Breaking: MiCA gave crypto a passport, but customers still face borders

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read | Sumber: https://cryptoslate.com/mica-gave-crypto-a-passport-but-customers-still-face-borders/

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Behind Europe's shiny fresh crypto passport lies a messy reality of uneven payment options, different legal entities, and customers navigating rules they rarely see.
  • Hungary scrapped an extra set of crypto restrictions in August, and for customers who had spent months wondering when they could trade normally again, that should have made things simpler.
  • But what they were told still depended on which app they used.

Behind Europe's shiny fresh crypto passport lies a messy reality of uneven payment options, different legal entities, and customers navigating rules they rarely see.

Hungary scrapped an extra set of crypto restrictions in August, and for customers who had spent months wondering when they could trade normally again, that should have made things simpler.

But what they were told still depended on which app they used.

Bitvavo declared that trading and euro deposits were returning for Hungarian customers, with newly introduced registrations reopening on Sept. 7. When checked on Nov. 13, Revolut's Hungarian help page still described the shutdown of its crypto services and account closures tied to a December 2025 deadline.

Support pages can outlive the restrictions they describe, so the notices show what each company published, while actual access would require an account or transaction test to verify.

The European Union spent years building a common framework so authorized crypto companies could expand without collecting a separate license in every country.

In a recent development, customers can still find different ways to fund an account across borders, or discover that the crypto and cash balances in the same app are handled by different companies under different rules. The EU's Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation (MiCA) leaves room for some of those differences and sets limits on others.

Sources indicate that miCA gives authorized crypto companies what's known as a passport. Under Article 59(7), a company can offer its approved services elsewhere in the EU without opening a local office. It tells its home regulator where it intends to operate and which services it prepares to offer.

Under Article 65, it can start once it receives confirmation that the information has been sent to the relevant authorities, or no later than 15 days after submitting it.

Industry observers note that revolut's crypto subsidiary received MiCA authorization in Cyprus in October 2025, and France's financial regulator lists it as authorized to offer crypto services in France under that same framework. The passport lets providers serve upcoming markets and decide where to offer each approved service.

Hungary complicated that process in 2025 when amendments to its crypto legislation added an extra requirement to validate crypto conversions, backed by criminal penalties.

Sources indicate that companies already authorized under MiCA now had an additional Hungarian requirement to meet. Revolut's instructions told customers to sell their crypto by Dec. 18, 2025, and remarked it would sell any remaining holdings automatically and close their crypto accounts.

On Jan. 30, the European Commission opened an infringement procedure, arguing that MiCA gave Hungary no basis for the extra authorization regime.

The Commission acknowledged Hungary's interest in preventing money laundering and argued that any measures it adopted had to comply with EU law. Hungary repealed the requirement before a court ruled on the dispute.

It has been revealed that act XXXVIII of 2026 took effect on Aug. 7, and its official explanatory memorandum acknowledged that the requirement was incompatible with EU crypto regulation. MiCA's maximum transitional period had already ended on July 1, 2026.

The repeal gave companies room to reopen services, as Bitvavo announced it would. Even then, its general eligibility page, updated on Nov. 4, omitted Hungary from its list of supported countries. Its dedicated reopening notice and country payment page both listed services for Hungarian customers.

The dedicated notice better explains what Bitvavo stated it would do in Hungary, although someone trying to work out whether they could sign up could read two pages from the same exchange and come away with different answers.

Once you have an account, the differences between countries often show up when you try to add money.

Recent findings suggest that coinbase's European payment guide lists Easy Bank Transfer for cash deposits in the Netherlands, Finland, France, Germany, and Ireland. It lists card deposits in the Netherlands, Italy, and Spain, while Polish customers can use BLIK to buy crypto directly.

In a recent development, buying crypto and depositing cash are separate entries in the guide, so when Germany is missing from the card deposit list, that tells you about funding an account. To see if you can buy crypto with a card, you'd check the purchase column.

According to recent reports, kraken's support documentation gives another example. Dutch residents can use iDEAL to deposit euros on Kraken, and withdrawals require a different method. These differences can come down to how an exchange has arranged to move money between a customer's bank and its platform.

Industry observers note that under Article 70(4), an exchange can handle associated payment services itself or use a partner, provided whoever handles the payments has the required authorization. The exchange must tell customers who provides the service and what terms apply.

In a recent development, miCA imposes separate duties on how companies give customers access to crypto services. Article 76 requires trading platforms to use objective, non-discriminatory access rules and proportionate participation requirements.

Recent findings suggest that their fees must also be transparent, fair, and non-discriminatory. Article 77 applies when a provider buys or sells crypto directly with customers using its own capital. It requires the provider to publish a non-discriminatory policy explaining whom it serves and what conditions customers have to meet.

Guidance published by the European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA) explains that the provider must fill an order once the customer meets the published conditions and the order becomes final.

To assess whether a provider has breached those duties, you'd need to compare customers asking for the same regulated service from the same legal entity, taking into account eligibility and any required compliance checks.

Coinbase's card deposit options in Germany and Italy and Kraken's rules for iDEAL tell you which payment methods are available. They give you only part of the information you'd need to make that comparison.

Rejecting an otherwise reachable EU bank account solely because its IBAN comes from another member state can amount to IBAN discrimination under SEPA rules. You'd need evidence that a provider refused an eligible account because of its IBAN. The public guides tell customers which local payment methods each exchange supports.

When you move between trading, payments, and rewards in the same app, you may be dealing with a different company on each screen.

Industry observers note that kraken's European Economic Area terms, effective Oct. 14, put its core crypto services under an Irish MiCA-authorized entity. Another Irish manufacturer handles electronic money, and a Cypriot investment firm provides derivatives and xStocks. The agreement also lists separate terms for staking and margin trading.

In a recent development, coinbase's European migration notice describes a similar split. Coinbase Luxembourg took over crypto services under its MiCA authorization, while Coinbase Ireland continued to provide electronic money services.

You can see both balances in the same account even though one company is responsible for the cash balance and another provides the crypto services. Each license covers the company that holds it and the activities that company has been authorized to carry out.

According to recent reports, staking reveals how protections can depend on what a provider does with your assets. MiCA has no separate staking regime, but if a provider holds your crypto or private keys while staking on your behalf, that custody activity is subject to MiCA's authorization and custody requirements.

Sources indicate that the European Commission explained how this works in guidance published through ESMA. ESMA has also warned that when a regulated company offers other products alongside its licensed services, customers can assume those products come with the same protections.

Industry observers note that under Article 66, companies must explain the services they offer accurately, with fair, understandable information that doesn't mislead customers. In Revolut's Hungarian case, readers of the old notice are left wondering whether the halt is still in effect and, if so, what's keeping it in place now that Hungary has repealed the validation rule.

To assess the notice under MiCA, a regulator would need to determine what Revolut currently offers in Hungary and why any restrictions remain in place.

Parts of the European market already work the same way across borders. Kraken's European restrictions page groups customers across the European Economic Area together for certain restrictions on assets and rewards. Hungarian customers trying to work out whether they can trade again have a different problem.

The law that prompted the shutdown is gone, but the information they need is specific to the exchange: whether it will accept their account, how they can fund it, and which company will handle their assets once they do.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • MEGA, the organization behind Ethereum Layer 2 network MegaETH, has reduced its workforce by 20% as it prepares to expand beyond blockchain infrastructure and develop artificial intelligence products.
  • It has been revealed that co-founder Shuyao Kong announced the restructuring on November 13, confirming that employees involved in the blockchain, wallet, and ecosystem teams were affected.
  • Industry observers note that the move comes shortly after the MegaETH Foundation rebranded as MEGA and committed $30 million from its treasury toward developing products on the network.

MEGA, the organization behind Ethereum Layer 2 network MegaETH, has reduced its workforce by 20% as it prepares to expand beyond blockchain infrastructure and develop artificial intelligence products.

It has been revealed that co-founder Shuyao Kong announced the restructuring on November 13, confirming that employees involved in the blockchain, wallet, and ecosystem teams were affected. The company did not disclose the exact number of positions eliminated, but said its founders, early employees, and core engineering team remain committed to the project.

Industry observers note that the move comes shortly after the MegaETH Foundation rebranded as MEGA and committed $30 million from its treasury toward developing products on the network. Its first major initiative is an AI marketplace scheduled for December.

Kong explained that the organization had spent several months reviewing its structure and strategic direction before deciding to reduce its workforce. The restructuring affected people who had contributed to developing MegaETH’s blockchain, wallet, and broader ecosystem. Some employees had reportedly been involved with the project since its early stages.

Kong noted the team no longer wanted to operate exclusively as a blockchain infrastructure company, arguing that doing so would mean overlooking a significant opportunity in artificial intelligence. The shift reflects MEGA’s intention to build products directly on its network rather than focus solely on providing the underlying technology for other applications.

The organization has committed $30 million from its existing treasury to support this strategy. AI services are expected to be the starting point, although the company has not disclosed how the funding will be distributed across its planned products.

MEGA’s first planned product is an AI inference marketplace that will allow customers to access services from competing AI model providers.

Industry observers note that AI inference refers to the process through which trained artificial intelligence models generate responses, predictions, or other outputs based on user requests. The proposed marketplace aims to make it easier for customers to compare and access different services.

According to the project’s white paper, the platform could introduce mechanisms allowing people to verify which models providers are actually using and reserve computing capacity at agreed prices.

Industry observers note that these features are intended to address concerns surrounding transparency, service reliability, and access to computing resources. However, MEGA has not confirmed which capabilities will be available when the marketplace releases or identified the providers and models expected to participate.

The strategic shift comes as activity across MegaETH’s decentralized finance ecosystem has declined considerably.

Data from DeFiLlama showed that the network’s total value locked (TVL) had fallen to approximately $8.8 million, down from a peak exceeding $245 million. The decline highlights the challenges MegaETH faces in maintaining liquidity and attracting activity to its blockchain applications. The MEGA token has also struggled, losing more than 70% of its value this year.

Initially developed as an Ethereum scaling solution focused on making blockchain applications, including trading platforms and games, faster, MegaETH is now seeking additional use cases through AI-related services.

The firm hopes that building products on its own infrastructure will create fresh demand for the network and expand its role beyond decentralized finance.

The workforce reduction and product expansion represent a significant change in direction for the organization behind MegaETH. Rather than concentrating primarily on blockchain infrastructure, MEGA is positioning itself at the intersection of decentralized technology and artificial intelligence.

However, the success of this approach will depend on whether the planned marketplace can attract customers, AI providers, and sufficient computing resources. Its proposed verification features will also need to demonstrate practical value before they can distinguish the platform from competing services.

MEGA has also indicated that its fresh products will operate on MegaETH, while the network continues working toward planned decentralization changes expected by the end of March 2027.

It has been revealed that the upcoming marketplace launch will therefore be an key milestone. It could help establish a new source of activity for the network, but the company still faces the challenge of rebuilding momentum after a substantial decline in DeFi participation.

Will decentralized AI marketplaces become an key use case for Ethereum scaling networks, or will established AI providers maintain their advantage?

XRP, Dogecoin, and Solana Doomed? Billionaire Tim Draper Predicts Altcoins Will Be Absorbed By Bitcoin — Here’s Why

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read | Sumber: https://zycrypto.com/xrp-dogecoin-and-solana-doomed-billionaire-tim-draper-predicts-altcoins-will-be-absorbed-by-bitcoin-heres-why/

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Could Ripple’s XRP, Dogecoin, and Solana eventually lose their place in the crypto market as Bitcoin strengthens its dominance?
  • Draper’s bold forecast raises fresh questions about the long-term survival of major digital assets and whether BTC’s growing influence could ultimately leave even established altcoins struggling to remain relevant.
  • Tim Draper has drawn a striking comparison between Bitcoin’s potential dominance and Microsoft’s rise to power in the software industry, arguing that the OG crypto could eventually absorb innovations pioneered by competing digital assets.

Could Ripple’s XRP, Dogecoin, and Solana eventually lose their place in the crypto market as Bitcoin strengthens its dominance? Billionaire investor Tim Draper believes the future of cryptocurrencies could look very different, predicting that altcoins will eventually be absorbed by Bitcoin.

Draper’s bold forecast raises fresh questions about the long-term survival of major digital assets and whether BTC’s growing influence could ultimately leave even established altcoins struggling to remain relevant.

Tim Draper has drawn a striking comparison between Bitcoin’s potential dominance and Microsoft’s rise to power in the software industry, arguing that the OG crypto could eventually absorb innovations pioneered by competing digital assets.

In a recent post on X, Draper suggested that Bitcoin could follow a similar path to Microsoft, which built its dominance not necessarily by inventing popular software applications but by incorporating successful innovations into its broader ecosystem.

It has been revealed that to illustrate his argument, Draper pointed to Microsoft’s handling of early software pioneers such as Lotus 1-2-3 and WordPerfect. Although these companies helped establish demand for spreadsheet and word-processing applications, Microsoft eventually introduced Excel and Word and integrated both into its operating system. The tech giant also acquired PowerPoint early on, turning the presentation software into another core part of its productivity suite.

According to Draper, this strategy allowed Microsoft to absorb successful ideas while the companies that initially popularized them gradually lost their competitive edge. He believes Bitcoin could follow the same playbook, with alternative cryptocurrencies serving as testing grounds for innovations that could eventually migrate to the Bitcoin network.

“Altcoins are the Lotus 1-2-3s and WordPerfects of this era,” Draper wrote, arguing that competing blockchain projects may demonstrate the value of fresh technologies before Bitcoin adopts them. In his view, Bitcoin’s powerful network effects and growing ecosystem could give it the gravitational pull needed to attract innovations from across the broader cryptocurrency industry.

It has been revealed that draper further supported his argument by highlighting Bitcoin’s expanding share of the overall cryptocurrency market. The billionaire recalled watching the flagship cryptocurrency’s market dominance climb from approximately 40% to 50% and eventually reach 61%. He views this steady increase as evidence of Bitcoin’s growing influence and its ability to strengthen its position despite the emergence of thousands of competing digital assets.

“Bitcoin is that platform,” Draper asserted.

If his prediction proves accurate, established altcoins such as Ripple-linked XRP, Dogecoin (DOGE), and Solana (SOL) could face an increasingly challenging competitive environment. Each has built its reputation around distinct use cases and communities, but Draper’s argument suggests that Bitcoin could eventually incorporate innovations that right now give these competing networks their appeal.

According to recent reports, for instance, XRP is best known for its focus on cross-border payments and the expanding financial ecosystem built around the XRP Ledger. Dogecoin, meanwhile, has evolved from an internet meme into one of the cryptocurrency market’s most recognizable assets, backed by a dedicated community. Solana, on the other hand, has established itself as a major smart contract platform, attracting developers with its high transaction speeds and relatively low fees while supporting a diverse ecosystem of decentralized finance (DeFi), NFTs, meme coins, and tokenized real-world assets.

Ultimately, Draper’s thesis is that these innovations could be a boon for BTC rather than guarantee the long-term dominance of the altcoins that pioneered or popularized them.

#491. Ethereum Staking Hits Record 36.3% Of Supply As ETH Holders Lock In

📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3 min read (640 words)

Ethereum Staking Hits Record 36.3% Of Supply As ETH Holders Lock In

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read | Sumber: https://bitcoinist.com/ethereum-staking-hits-record-36-3-of-supply-as-eth-holders-lock-in/

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The ETH price has had a rough month.
  • Recent findings suggest that more than a third of all ether is now locked in staking, a latest all-time high.
  • That is a jump of nearly four percentage points in just five months, and it happened while the market was falling.

The ETH price has had a rough month. But Ethereum’s most committed holders do not seem to care.

Recent findings suggest that more than a third of all ether is now locked in staking, a latest all-time high. According to Token Terminal data, Ethereum’s staking rate has climbed to 36.3% of total supply, up from the previous record of 32.4% set in June 2026.

That is a jump of nearly four percentage points in just five months, and it happened while the market was falling.

Staking is more than a way to earn yield. Validators lock up ETH to verify transactions, propose upcoming blocks and keep Ethereum’s proof-of-stake system running. The more ETH that is staked, the more expensive it becomes to attack the network.

It also changes the supply picture. Staked ETH cannot be sold instantly, so every coin that enters staking leaves the pool of ETH readily available on the market.

With more than one-third of supply now committed, a large share of ether is effectively off the table for traders.

According to recent reports, the validator queues suggest the trend is not slowing down. Reports show that about 2.42 million ETH is currently waiting to start staking, with an estimated wait time of around 42 days.

It has been revealed that the exit queue, meanwhile, sits at zero. In other words, far more ETH is trying to get into staking than out of it.

According to recent reports, that is a dramatic reversal from late 2025. In September of that year, the exit backlog peaked near 2.67 million ETH before collapsing to almost nothing by January 2026.

The network now counts roughly 897,000 active validators, with stakers earning an annual rate of about 2.6%.

In a recent development, much of the growth has come from large players. Ethereum treasury firm BitMine has steadily added to its staked position, while staking features in spot Ether ETFs have opened the door for traditional investors to earn yield on their holdings.

Recent findings suggest that as reported earlier this year, BitMine and Grayscale were among the institutions driving staking to record levels. That trend has only accelerated since.

Recent findings suggest that history also offers some comfort. Analysts at XWIN Research Japan, writing on CryptoQuant, noted that Ethereum staking levels continued to climb even during the sharp corrections of 2022 and 2023.

Industry observers note that the contrast with the price is striking. ETH is trading near $2,000, down roughly 18% over the past month. Bitcoin’s drop below $70,000 and outflows from spot Ether ETFs have weighed on the whole market.

But staking tells a different story. While short-term traders head for the exits, long-term holders are locking up more ETH than ever. That gap between price and network commitment is exactly what some investors watch for, as supply tightens quietly underneath a weak chart.

It also echoes other signals flashing near this zone, including an Ethereum metric that has never missed a bottom. If demand returns, a smaller pool of liquid ETH could amplify the move higher. For more updates, follow the latest Ethereum news.

Is record Ethereum staking a sign that ETH is quietly building a bottom, or will price keep ignoring the network’s growth for now?

#492. Industry News: Wall Street wants 24/7 trading, but somebody has to bankroll the weekend

📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11 min read (2185 words)
General

Industry News: Wall Street wants 24/7 trading, but somebody has to bankroll the weekend

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read | Sumber: https://cryptoslate.com/wall-street-wants-24-7-trading-but-somebody-has-to-bankroll-the-weekend/

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Wall Street is getting closer to trading around the clock, but the institutions behind those trades still have to find the cash to keep everything moving when settlement has to wait.
  • Wall Street's move toward round-the-clock trading includes a key decision about who supplies cash when the main wholesale payment systems are closed.
  • If you want to adjust a position on Saturday, being able to trade saves you from waiting until Monday.

Wall Street is getting closer to trading around the clock, but the institutions behind those trades still have to find the cash to keep everything moving when settlement has to wait.

Wall Street's move toward round-the-clock trading includes a key decision about who supplies cash when the main wholesale payment systems are closed.

If you want to adjust a position on Saturday, being able to trade saves you from waiting until Monday. The companies behind your trade still have to manage what they owe until they can settle, and they have to decide how much more business they can take on before they can replenish their cash or collateral.

Industry observers note that CME opened its crypto derivatives markets on weekends in May, but kept settlement on a business-day schedule. Some stablecoin providers give customers faster access to cash by putting money at partner banks in advance.

Both arrangements give investors more hours to act, but they also mean different companies are now responsible for ensuring the money is available when needed.

We saw an example of what happens when the wait gets longer in June. Two major DTCC subsidiaries postponed a day's securities settlement, leaving cash in the central counterparty's account at the Fed and reducing the reserves available to banks.

The companies involved got through the delay without the jump in short-term rates that the Chicago Fed later described as a possible consequence. Longer trading hours ask companies to be ready for similar delays when their usual sources of cash and operational support may be harder to reach.

It has been revealed that when an institution buys and sells securities through DTCC's clearing subsidiary NSCC, it can use what it's owed on its sales to offset what it owes on its purchases. NSCC stands between buyers and sellers in eligible trades, which lets it work out what each firm owes across all those transactions.

DTCC says that process, called multilateral netting, cuts equity payment obligations by an average of 98%. That reduces the amount companies have to pay at settlement.

Illustration per $100 of equity payment obligations before netting. DTCC reports a 98% average reduction. About $2 remains payable per $100, calculated as $100 minus $98.

Companies still have to make the remaining payments once those trades are netted. According to DTCC's June 30 incident notice, a participant submitted erroneous trades the previous day, creating an unusually large payment obligation.

DTC and NSCC invoked their market-disruption rules and got several extensions from the Federal Reserve while they tried to reverse the trades. They ran out of time at the final 8:30 p.m. deadline and carried the balances into June 30.

It has been revealed that settlement for both days went through on June 30, but the delay had already left companies with bills to cover. NSCC added a start-of-day charge to its risk fund to cover another day of trades it had guaranteed, and companies expecting payments had to wait for their money.

Cash had accumulated in the central counterparty's account at the Fed, where it stayed until settlement could send it back to the banks due to receive it.

Banks' balances at the Fed are called reserves. Some companies that clear and settle trades also have Fed accounts, and their balances are recorded separately.

Suppose banks send $10 billion to one of those companies and an operational problem holds up the payments back to them. All else equal, bank reserves fall by $10 billion, and the firm's Fed balance rises by the same amount.

The cash is still at the Fed, but it's in an account the banks can't draw on to make payments.

The Chicago Fed described that in its November account of the disruption, but it didn't put a dollar figure on the decline in reserves. Cindy Hull, a Chicago Fed official, offered two possible reasons short-term rates held steady: companies trusted the payments would go through, and the banking system had enough reserves to handle the temporary drop.

DTCC's July 9 follow-up described who would bear some of the costs. Companies still owed money would receive interest based on what DTCC earned on the cash overnight, and those that owed money wouldn't face financing charges.

DTCC would consider claims case by case when losses tied directly to the delay materially exceeded the interest payment.

CME's 24/7 schedule covers cryptocurrency futures and options, except spot-quoted futures, with at least two hours of weekly maintenance.

According to recent reports, under its implementation notice, trades made from Friday evening through Sunday evening are booked for the next business day, when clearing and settlement are processed. DTCC has made a similar move with NSCC trade processing, which has run 24 hours a day, five days a week since June 28.

The exchange can take a weekend trade before its clearing and settlement systems process it.

CME assigns covered weekend crypto trades to the next business day, when it processes clearing and settlement.

Recent findings suggest that this diagram covers CME's published schedule for eligible contracts. The gap varies by trade time and holidays. The arrow highlights sequence.

CME's May 18, 2026 Globex notice specifies the trade-date and processing schedule for covered cryptocurrency futures and options.

This diagram covers CME's published schedule for eligible contracts. The gap varies by trade time and holidays. The arrow shows sequence.

In a recent development, your Bitcoin position can lose value over the weekend whether the futures exchange is open or closed. When the exchange is open, you can cut that exposure, and the companies clearing the trades must decide how much latest risk customers can take before the next settlement.

Sources indicate that thanks for signing up to The Catalyst. Look out for your first daily email. If you already receive it, you’re all set.

Nodal set out two ways to do that for selected Coinbase derivatives in a May 2025 filing.

In the first option, members must keep additional weekend trading below half the customer's excess margin, which is the collateral left over once existing requirements are met. In the second, customers can use all of that excess margin, minus any losses on positions they still hold.

Gains on those positions only count toward buying power once margin is recalculated after the weekend. Members that support weekend contracts also pay a surcharge into the guaranty fund. The idea is to keep customers from adding positions with money they're still waiting to receive.

In a recent development, the Federal Reserve's approved expansion will add Sundays and weekday holidays to Fedwire Funds and the National Settlement Service no earlier than 2028. The latest schedule still runs Sunday through Friday, with daily hours of 22 and 21.5, respectively.

FedNow already runs through the weekend, but its transaction limit rose to $10 million in November 2025, well below what some clearing companies need to move.

According to recent reports, chicago Fed researcher David DeCarlo looked at CME's quarterly disclosures from the third quarter of 2022 through the third quarter of 2025. Each quarter, CME's base clearing service reported the largest payment any one participant had owed over the previous year. The median of those reported figures was $3.73 billion.

Recent findings suggest that the median estimate under severe but plausible conditions was $24.31 billion. Both numbers cover a much broader business than weekend crypto trading, and some payments can be offset when companies use the same settlement bank.

While they're not perfect representations of the market, they show why payment size can be as notable as the hours the network is open.

CME base clearing service. Medians of quarterly disclosures from Q3 2022 through Q3 2025. Actual figures are the largest single-participant payment obligation reported for the preceding year. Stress estimates reflect extreme but plausible conditions. The figures cover the broader clearing service and measure neither typical payments nor weekend crypto funding needs.

Source: Chicago Fed Letter No. 519, Figure 2.

It has been revealed that you can send stablecoins that are already in circulation between wallets outside banking hours, provided the recipient can accept them. If they need dollars in a bank account, the next step is to redeem the tokens.

In an October explanation of its redemption service, Circle stated qualified platform customers and customers using its payments network could redeem around the clock and receive money in near real time. Standard routes typically take up to two business days.

Circle says it can do that because it keeps cash ready at partner banks and has arrangements to move it when customers need it. The cash earns less than it would in Treasuries, so Circle gives up some interest to offer faster redemptions.

How well the service holds up when more customers than expected want their money depends on how much cash those banks can deliver.

Tokenized securities can also move outside banking hours once they've been converted into tokens. Already-tokenized securities can move at any hour between registered wallets on the same blockchain.

DTCC's launch plan keeps conversion orders on business-day hours and puts digital cash and on-chain netting on an indicative roadmap for later. If you expect to post tokenized collateral over the weekend, you may need to prepare it in advance and confirm the recipient will accept it.

Sources indicate that on Nov. 11, OKXICE, a joint venture between OKX and the owner of the Newly introduced York Stock Exchange, announced a Nov. 23 launch for round-the-clock trading in more than 70 expected tokenized securities, including 59 Direxion ETFs.

According to recent reports, eligible US customers would trade through permissioned liquidity pools on X Layer, and the exchange would rely on a temporary SEC exemption. The launch announcement leaves open when the related banking and redemption services would be available.

When someone sends you an asset to settle a trade, you need to know when the transfer is final and whether you can use what you received.

International standards for systemically key stablecoin arrangements address both points. They cover when a transfer becomes legally irrevocable and whether a holder can redeem the stablecoin at face value under stress.

Now imagine a payment goes wrong at 3 a.m. on Saturday. The sender's records show the payment instruction went through, but the recipient still has no money it can spend.

While staff work out whether the problem is a delayed message or a failed transfer, someone has to decide whether the company can spare cash for a replacement payment and what it can still afford to settle if the original payment goes through later.

The CFTC's May 29 advisory on continuous trading explains what trading platforms should have in place under existing rules.

It covers who needs to be on hand across operations and risk, how companies respond to disruptions, whether they can reach the vendors they depend on, and how platforms can use parallel systems to upgrade or roll back software while keeping trading open.

When a payment gets stuck, the people who can authorize a replacement also need to reach the bank or counterparty that can deliver it.

The companies involved in June's disruption got through an extra day without a jump in short-term rates. Weekend trading gives investors more ways to manage their exposure, and it forces companies to handle a delay like that while customers are still adding positions.

If an expected payment gets held up on Saturday, somebody needs enough cash to cover what comes due next, and the authority to release it before the usual payment systems reopen.

  • According to recent reports, cryptoSlate matched 31 validators marked retired from the program to active vote accounts.
  • Thirty-one Solana validators marked “Retired” by the Solana Foundation’s delegation program were still voting in a Nov.
  • The finding sharpens the question facing smaller validators under the Foundation’s published 12-month membership model: whether they can replace program support with other delegation.

According to recent reports, cryptoSlate matched 31 validators marked retired from the program to active vote accounts. Two accounted for just over half of the cohort’s stake.

Thirty-one Solana validators marked “Retired” by the Solana Foundation’s delegation program were still voting in a Nov. 14 snapshot. They carried 63 million SOL in delegated stake, about 15% of active stake in the voting accounts CryptoSlate examined.

The finding sharpens the question facing smaller validators under the Foundation’s published 12-month membership model: whether they can replace program support with other delegation.

According to recent reports, cryptoSlate compared the Foundation’s participant register with voting data from Solana’s mainnet RPC endpoint, captured at approximately 05:15 UTC on November 14, 2026. The accompanying epoch response placed the observation at epoch 1086.

CryptoSlate identified 31 retired-program validators in current vote accounts with active stake. They carried 63 million SOL of the 429 million SOL across 663 such accounts, or 14.8% using the unrounded amounts.

According to recent reports, those SOL totals describe stake delegated to the voting accounts, rather than the validators’ beneficial ownership of the tokens. The denominator is the selected current voting set, rather than SOL’s circulating supply or the Foundation’s own stake.

The result establishes participation at the observation time. It does not establish that these validators retired under the current membership rules, or that the published membership rules caused their continued operation.

The Foundation’s delegation FAQ defines retirement as the end of membership in the Solana Foundation Delegation Program, or SFDP, and claims retired validators no longer receive its stake delegations. It also says retirement is not a penalty or performance violation, and validators may continue operating on the permissionless network.

According to recent reports, the FAQ describes a 12-month term measured from the first epoch a validator was eligible for a Foundation delegation on mainnet. It also specifies retirement when stake from outside SFDP exceeds 300,000 SOL and offers retiring or retired members an application route for renewal.

The Foundation publishes two different thresholds. Its delegation criteria still say a validator retires above 1 million SOL in outside stake, while the FAQ states 300,000 SOL. The criteria’s current mainnet table is labeled epoch 1085; neither page resolves which cutoff the Foundation applies in practice.

In a recent development, program status, eligibility and actual funding also need to remain distinct. Approved onboarding makes a validator eligible for support, while performance requirements govern delegation and stake can take epochs to become active. Membership status alone therefore cannot identify how much Foundation stake an individual validator received.

The active retired cohort is concentrated: its two largest identities accounted for 52.5% of the cohort’s stake. Fourteen of the 31 identities had less than 300,000 SOL of total activated stake. That is a different measure from the FAQ’s external-stake threshold, and neither figure establishes profitability.

#497. Why Binance’s ‘kill switch’ couldn’t stop hackers from draining $6.3B — Explained!

Why Binance’s ‘kill switch’ couldn’t stop hackers from draining $6.3B — Explained!

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read | Sumber: https://ambcrypto.com/why-binances-kill-switch-couldnt-stop-hackers-from-draining-6-3b-explained/

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes.
  • In a recent development, read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes.
  • There is a certain irony in pulling the emergency brake, only to discover that the machinery you’re trying to stop is operating beyond your reach.

It has been revealed that read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

In a recent development, read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

There is a certain irony in pulling the emergency brake, only to discover that the machinery you’re trying to stop is operating beyond your reach.

Binance encountered a rather expensive version of that problem on 29th October. Attackers compromised its wallet signing infrastructure and obtained authority to move cryptocurrency through mechanisms that did not depend on the exchange’s ordinary withdrawal process. Suspending withdrawals could interrupt that process. It could do considerably less about permissions already established on Ethereum.

By the time the attack was contained, approximately $6.3 billion had been stolen and Binance’s engineers had developed a specialised procedure to revoke malicious on-chain authority. The exchange could shut down affected services, but Ethereum would continue recognising the delegation until it was explicitly cleared.

Brian Cubellis, Chief Strategy Officer at Bitcoin custody platform Onramp, offered his two cents to AMBCrypto,.

Pausing withdrawals turns off the exchange’s own software, but it does nothing about permissions the attacker has already written to the blockchain.

The distinction is an uncomfortable one for an institution entrusted with billions in customer assets.

It has been revealed that binance subsequently coordinated freezes of stolen funds and began replenishing the affected holdings, reporting approximately 98% replenishment by 4th November. Its financial response was substantial.

However, it still is worth questioning what remained possible while its emergency controls were taking effect.

By the way, for those unaware, the attack began well before 29th October and nowhere near a blockchain.

Sources indicate that according to Binance’s 3rd November incident report, an engineer downloaded a tampered installation package for an AI coding tool in June. The exchange detected the anomaly and replaced the device, but the attackers had already gathered intelligence about its employees and infrastructure. Well into September, another engineer was approached through a fictitious recruitment process involving interviews and a malicious coding assignment.

By 20th October, the attackers had used compromised employee systems and internal AI tooling to access additional machines. In doing so, they ultimately obtained credentials that opened the way to Binance’s wallet signing infrastructure.

In a recent development, it all paid off on the 29th. Between 20:05 and 20:09 UTC, hot wallets transferred approximately 223.46 million XRP, 970,500 SOL and 44.2 million OP to attacker controlled addresses. Bitcoin and other assets followed. Chainalysis subsequently estimated the overall theft at approximately $6.4 billion.

What was the most consequential part of this intrusion though? The attackers gained access to Binance’s signing infrastructure, the very machinery responsible for authorizing transactions.

On Ethereum, the attackers exploited EIP-7702, a mechanism that allows an externally owned account to delegate execution to smart-contract code.

It has been revealed that ordinarily, that flexibility expands what a wallet can do. Here, according to Binance, the compromised signing infrastructure was used to grant malicious code execution rights over an Ethereum hot wallet. The exchange described 50 signed transactions involved in manipulating the account’s nonce and establishing the delegation.

Industry observers note that the unsettling part comes next though. Those permissions remained valid on-chain even after Binance suspended withdrawals and shut down its hot-wallet services. The exchange could stop its own systems from processing transactions, but it could not simply switch off the authority the attackers had already established on Ethereum.

It has been revealed that then came another complication. Binance’s hot wallet used multi-party computation (MPC), which distributes the production of cryptographic signatures across multiple participants or components rather than relying on a single conventional private key. That architecture can reduce certain risks, but it also meant there was no single private key available to revoke the malicious delegation immediately.

In a recent development, binance’s engineers had to DEVELOP a specialised revocation procedure while the incident was UNFOLDING. Of course, this took additional time, prolonging the effort to contain unauthorized asset movements.

In a recent development, at 23:56 UTC, the final reported unauthorized Ethereum transfer, involving 2,961.9 ETH, was confirmed on-chain. Binance said it had been broadcast earlier and remained pending before confirmation. At 00:10 UTC on 30th October, the exchange cleared the malicious EIP-7702 delegation with a fresh authorization to the zero address.

Sources indicate that the distinction between broadcast and confirmation matters. So does the absence of an established total for funds transferred after withdrawals were suspended.

Binance acknowledged that suspension alone could not stop every unauthorized movement, but its disclosures do not establish a reconciled post-suspension loss figure.

In a recent development, there is a comforting simplicity to the idea of a kill switch. Something goes wrong, someone pulls the plug and the damage stops. Unfortunately, the blockchain has no particular obligation to respect an exchange’s internal emergency procedures.

Recent findings suggest that consider a hotel discovering that someone has obtained an unauthorized key card. Closing reception prevents new cards from being issued. The existing card still opens the door. Cancelling it, securing the valuables, and recovering what has already disappeared are separate jobs.

Now, this comparison has its limits, but it captures the dilemma facing exchanges whose wallet permissions outlive their own systems.

The problem surfaced in a public exchange between Haseeb Qureshi, Managing Partner at Dragonfly, and  Tudor Anastasiu. Tudor Anastasiu is a blockchain infrastructure and security engineer and the founder of Anastasiu Labs.

The disagreement exposes a distinction that is easy to overlook in the middle of a breach.

According to recent reports, A defensive sweep can move assets to safety, provided the exchange can authorize and execute it before the attacker does. However, moving funds does not necessarily invalidate permissions already granted on-chain and it certainly cannot retrieve assets that have already disappeared.

So, that leaves a rather awkward question: If the signing infrastructure itself has been compromised, how does an exchange authorize an emergency transaction without trusting the very system it suspects?

Carlos Vendrell, Founder of Zealynx Security, sees the answer in testing the procedure under exactly those conditions.

The drill should start from a list of every approval and delegation each hot wallet has given, then revoke one of them for real while assuming the normal signing service is the compromised part, and time it.

Binance’s experience does not establish that MPC inherently prevents rapid revocation. Nor does its disclosure prove that no emergency procedure existed before the breach.

However, it does establish that engineers developed a specialised procedure during the incident and doing so took additional time.

Industry observers note that there was another complication here, one that made the situation look almost absurd. The compromised wallet was reportedly STILL receiving money.

In an analysis dated 4th November, Four Pillars reported that Binance’s deposit-consolidation system continued collecting funds into a compromised Ethereum wallet identified as Binance 14. This allowed the attacker to sweep newly arriving assets.

Nexus Mutual’s reconstruction offers a particularly striking sequence.

At approximately 21:44 UTC, it says the attacker swept 200 million USDT that another Binance-labelled wallet had deposited roughly 72 seconds earlier. Seventy-two seconds! Barely enough time to make a cup of coffee, yet apparently sufficient for a fresh transfer to reach a compromised address and disappear.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers’ findings raise a problem distinct from EIP-7702. An exchange can work to revoke an attacker’s authority while other operational systems continue directing funds towards a dangerous destination. Interrupting those internal asset flows is another containment task and requires its own controls and confirmation.

According to Brian Cubellis, emergency preparedness must account for the loss of the usual signing infrastructure.

An exchange should prove, before it is attacked, that it can cancel any permission on its wallets and move exposed funds to safety even if its own signing system has been taken over.

That is easier prescribed than engineered though.

An independent emergency signing path may accelerate recovery, but it also introduces powerful authority that must be secured. Build too much dependence into the ordinary system and the emergency route may fail alongside it. Concentrate too much authority in the alternative and the supposed safeguard becomes another attractive target.

Once stolen assets leave the exchange’s immediate control, containment becomes a race involving investigators, stablecoin issuers, blockchain networks and the attacker.

Chainalysis’s investigation also described an attempt to move approximately $500 million in stablecoins through a swapping address. Within roughly 20 minutes, the attackers reportedly converted around $325 million into assets less susceptible to issuer freezes, including Ether. The remaining $175 million was frozen.

It has been revealed that there was a reason for the rush. Stablecoin issuers such as Tether and Circle can freeze certain tokens at designated addresses. Bitcoin and Ether, by contrast, have no equivalent central issuer with that power. Converting the stolen stablecoins into other assets could therefore put them beyond the reach of an issuer-imposed freeze.

It has been revealed that this whole episode illustrates the limits of intervention once funds have escaped. Investigators may be able to follow the money on-chain, but knowing where it has gone does not necessarily give them the power to retrieve it.

Binance nevertheless managed to secure a substantial portion of the stolen assets. In its 3rd November report, the exchange noted that approximately $2.85 billion had been frozen or intercepted through cooperation with issuers, law enforcement, and blockchain intelligence firms. By 4th November, it reported replenishing approximately 98% of the affected holdings through replacement purchases.

Industry observers note that of course, Binance had demonstrated considerable capacity to absorb the losses rather than pass them on to people. However, it tells us how much the exchange managed to secure or replace, not how effectively it prevented the attacker from continuing to move assets during the breach.

A year earlier, Bybit had encountered a different version of the problem with compromised transaction authority. In February 2025, attackers stole approximately $1.5 billion after compromising the environment associated with its Safe{Wallet} approval process.

Recent findings suggest that according to Bybit’s forensic disclosure, malicious changes deceived signers into approving an unauthorized transaction. It also stated that investigators found no indication that its own infrastructure had been compromised.

Sources indicate that both incidents exposed how much depends on the integrity of the authority behind a transaction. Multiple signatures offer limited protection when signers are misled about what they are approving. And as Binance discovered, shutting down a signing service does not necessarily invalidate authority already established on-chain.

It has been revealed that an emergency kill switch sounds reassuring. Rather less reassuring is discovering, halfway through a breach, that the attacker has permissions your switch cannot revoke.

Binance’s experience raises an uncomfortable question for exchanges entrusted with billions in customer assets — Have they actually tested what happens when the systems responsible for protecting those assets become part of the attack?

An exchange should be able to demonstrate that it can revoke compromised permissions, move exposed assets to safety, and interrupt internal transfers without relying entirely on infrastructure it can no longer trust.

In a recent development, but what should customers make of an exchange’s public assurances when a breach is underway? AMBCrypto put that question to Vik Sharma, Founder and CEO of Cake Wallet,.

A useful update names which approvals were revoked, which assets moved, and where, so customers can check it themselves.

There are legitimate reasons to withhold sensitive operational details while an intrusion is underway. Once the immediate danger has passed, however, an exchange should be able to explain what its emergency controls actually stopped, when compromised authority was extinguished, and whether any assets remained exposed.

Industry observers note that binance deserves credit for publishing details of its response, coordinating substantial asset freezes, and committing its own resources to replenish affected holdings. Those measures helped absorb the financial damage. However, they also revealed why reimbursement and containment should never be confused.

A kill switch should buy defenders control, not merely time to figure out where control has gone.

As of the time of writing, XRP is trading around $0.9892, representing a substantial decline of about 3.94% over the past 24 hours and an 11.3% drop over the last week.

On 29th October, the largest hack in crypto’s history took Bitcoin to a low near $76,200. A few days later, on 5th November, an AI-driven tech crash spilled into crypto. The Nasdaq 100 fell by 6.4%, while semiconductor stocks tumbled by 12%.

This chaos set off leveraged liquidations of roughly $1.1 billion and pushed Bitcoin’s price below $74,000.

In a recent development, two different shocks, a historical Binance breach, and an AI token sell-off. Though they seem unrelated on the surface, this time they were actually the catalyst for the same event. What Bitcoin saw was a surge in speculative positioning, but what the king coin did not see was a buyer.

According to recent reports, the market’s first take on the Binance hack was that crypto had passed a test. Bitcoin fell by about 6% from its 28th October close — a fraction of the 15% to 39% drawdowns after the controversies surrounding Celsius, FTX, BlockFi, and Bybit.

Matt Mena, Crypto Research Strategist at 21Shares, told AMBCrypto,.

Industry observers note that what we find most encouraging is how the market handled the worst of it. The largest hack in crypto’s history caused a far smaller drawdown than past crises; the protocols kept running, and none of the structural drivers broke.

Recent findings suggest that unfortunately, institutional resilience is not retail demand. The market simply treated a smaller slump as evidence of Bitcoin’s underlying strength. However, whether anyone wanted to buy Bitcoin [BTC] was a separate question, one the hack never answered.

Recent findings suggest that still, institutional strength hasn’t eased the feeling of dread felt by many retail investors. And, a major factor can explain why.

Industry observers note that the most important signal is what happened after the liquidations: Nothing. Bitget Wallet’s analysts put it plainly that the leverage reset “has cleared some speculative excess, but is yet to address the underlying demand problem.”.

Looking at the data, one can see why. Most importantly, the ETF flows changed drastically. There were $2.6 billion worth of inflows in September 2026, which turned into $290 million of net outflows in October. Presently, U.S ETF holders sit underwater below their cost basis of $82K.

How ETF holders behave below breakeven remains the key tell for November.

Also, stablecoin supply has not been moving outside the $305 billion zone, a sure sign that liquidity is sitting still.

Finally, one cannot forget the fallout caused by the Binance hack.

According to recent reports, when the exchange reopened withdrawals, the queue moved fast. The exchange processed $4.65 billion against $1.01 billion of deposits in under ten hours; net outflows reached about $5.8 billion over 24 hours!

Each of these factors may not matter when seen separately, but when read together, they describe the same thing — capital leaving or sitting still. The leverage is gone, and the bid is not there to replace it.

For 21Shares, $73,000 is the 200-day moving average, and “the line that would reopen the bear-market debate.”.

Bitget analysts told AMBCrypto that Bitcoin must hold the $73K–$74K range.

The 73,000-74,000 range is now the zone Bitcoin needs to hold. Stabilization would require more balanced derivatives positioning and sustained positive ETF flows. Reclaiming and holding $80,000 would signal stronger demand, while a decisive break below $73,000 could expose $68,000. If $68,000 also fails to hold, the selloff would suggest more than a temporary leverage flush.

When the same number pops up again and again, it stops being a coincidence and starts pointing to a pattern — that Bitcoin is either in a temporary flush or at the start of something deeper.

If buyers do return, Bitcoin can comfortably start holding $80,000, and stronger demand would emerge as a result. Getting back above $81,000 to $82,000 would finally put the largest holder cohorts back in profit.

Recent findings suggest that both reports are similarly aligned on what won’t fix Bitcoin’s buyer problem: Macro relief without demand. In fact, Bitget’s analysts asserted,.

A durable Bitcoin recovery will depend on improving liquidity and Spot demand, not macro relief alone.

Matt Mena framed the same requirement as a four-part checklist.

Sources indicate that we are watching four things into November: Bitcoin holding $76,000 to $78,000 and reclaiming $80,000 to $82,000, Binance completing withdrawals and proving its reserves, credit spreads, oil and long-end yields, and whether ETF flows return. If those turn, the setup for the final weeks of the year remains constructive.

Sources indicate that notice what’s on both lists: ETF flows, liquidity, Spot demand, and positioning. All of them are things buyers have to do.

Industry observers note that there is naturally no doubt that macro factors can move Bitcoin’s price. If everything aligns, a rally can happen tomorrow. However, seasoned investors know that this will never be the same as rebuilding buyer interest.

Ultimately, a macro relief rally would leave Bitcoin’s demand problem exactly where it was.

According to recent reports, the calendar offers a boost for Bitcoin regardless of which way the ball drops, as December’s Fed expectations hinge on U.S CPI and PPI readings. For the uninitiated, hotter readings will reinforce rate-hike expectations, and a softer core inflation will trigger a relief rally.

However, Bitget’s analysts draw a line between the two outcomes, noting,.

In a recent development, this week’s inflation data adds another test. Hotter readings could reinforce December rate-hike expectations, while softer core inflation could trigger a relief rally. But a durable Bitcoin recovery will depend on improving liquidity and spot demand, not macro relief alone.

Basically, a relief rally can be classed as a macro event, not a demand event. The inflation print can only deliver the former, and the latter can only come about by real flows.

Here, it’s also worth being precise about what the 5th November AI crash tells us. 21Shares calls it,.

A renewed wobble in artificial intelligence (AI) equities pulled the Nasdaq-100 down almost 4%.

In a recent development, that’s the mechanism in a nutshell. Even this time, crypto’s fall was the result of trading alongside a risk asset.

In a recent development, still, if Bitcoin’s move below $74,000 was driven by the AI wipeout, then the absence of a bid is more telling. Eventually, we come back to the same problem of missing buyers.

Leverage has been reset twice in a week — Once by Binance’s $6.3 billion hack, once by an AI shocker. And the buyer bid has hardly appeared either time.

Recent findings suggest that that’s what makes $73,000 a critical level to watch. If buyers return and hold this level, they could help Bitcoin reclaim $80,000. This would also imply that BTC’s demand problem is cyclical, not permanent.

However, a break below $73,000 will hint at — and a failure at $68,000 will confirm — that Bitcoin’s breakdown is structural. Bitcoin’s recovery hinges on a single level, and the lack of buyers has never been felt stronger.

For years, investors in the crypto market have followed a familiar pattern. The moment they see that Bitcoin’s price gains are eventually slowing down, they begin moving capital into Ethereum and other altcoins in search of higher returns.

This rotation has historically fueled what the market calls an “altcoin season.”.

Recent findings suggest that however, 2026 is beginning to challenge that expectation. Though the market has seen brief periods of outperformance, these have failed to develop into a sustained rally across the wider altcoin ecosystem.

What makes this particularly concerning is that the year is now approaching its end without a convincing sign of the long-awaited rotation.

To understand the case better first, let’s focus on the total altcoin market capitalization, which fell from approximately $1.85 trillion to $1.06 trillion in just a month, erasing almost around $800 billion in value.

At the same time, the Altcoin Season Index has struggled to maintain readings above the 75 threshold, which traditionally signals an altcoin season.

At press time, too, the index was sitting at 48, which means that the Bitcoin [BTC] season continues to be in full swing at the moment despite BTC trading at $73,836.99 at press time.

This came after a recent report by AMBCrypto, which indicated that the median altcoin’s returns by November had dropped slightly below Bitcoin and that both Bitcoin’s 60-day returns and the altcoin’s returns had returned to zero.

Recent findings suggest that going back in time, the years 2021 and 2023 delivered substantial rallies during different parts of the year. However, the year 2022 remained dominated by bearish sentiment. Moving forward, the end of 2024 is what provides an notable point of comparison.

Following Bitcoin’s move above $100,000 in December, market attention expanded towards Ethereum [ETH], XRP, Solana, and other large-cap altcoins. And the broader market entered 2025 with considerable optimism around a potential continuation of that rotation.

However, the experience of 2025 also demonstrated that such rallies are not necessarily sustained. Glassnode’s historical analysis highlighted that altcoin trading volume had previously surged to nearly four times Bitcoin’s volume around September 2025, before cooling as Bitcoin approached its October market top.

Unlike Mini Apps, which open a web page on demand, widgets run inside the message itself. Telegram's widget documentation describes an isolated environment that runs their code on the user's device without direct internet access. Requests to the bot pass through Telegram instead.

Telegram's changelog describes widget queries involving a user's TON wallet card, wallet-signed data or notification of a wallet transaction. Those capabilities explain the relevance for crypto users, but do not themselves demonstrate unauthorized signing or asset theft.

  • The South Korean crypto exchange said potentially exposed information includes passwords, bank account numbers, national identification numbers and crypto wallet addresses.
  • South Korean crypto exchange Coinone warned customers of potential phishing scams and identity theft after an attacker breached its outsourced customer support provider, exposing information shared during customer service interactions.
  • On Sunday, Coinone said an attacker accessed servers operated by MetaM on Thursday and viewed or extracted customer support records.

The South Korean crypto exchange said potentially exposed information includes passwords, bank account numbers, national identification numbers and crypto wallet addresses.

South Korean crypto exchange Coinone warned customers of potential phishing scams and identity theft after an attacker breached its outsourced customer support provider, exposing information shared during customer service interactions.

On Sunday, Coinone said an attacker accessed servers operated by MetaM on Thursday and viewed or extracted customer support records. Coinone said it learned about the breach in the same day.

According to Coinone, the information potentially exposed names, phone numbers, email addresses, dates of birth, bank account numbers, passwords, national identification numbers, home and wallet addresses and transaction IDs.

Coinone mentioned the affected data varies by customer, and people who never contacted its support center were unaffected. It did not disclose how many customers were affected.

The exchange urged customers who shared passwords during support interactions to change them and warned that fraudsters could impersonate Coinone using details from previous conversations.

Coinone noted its account, trading and wallet infrastructure operates separately from MetaM’s servers, with no evidence of direct compromise. The exchange said it has reported the incident to South Korean authorities.

Industry observers note that the disclosure comes as South Korea moves to strengthen financial-sector cybersecurity. In October, the Financial Services Commission identified security deficiencies at 130 of 555 financial firms reviewed.

On Thursday, the regulator mentioned it would allow crypto exchanges to suspend withdrawals when hacking is suspected, alongside calls for round-the-clock monitoring.

Lorie Logan wants emergency support for Treasury markets while favoring further rate hikes, leaving Bitcoin exposed to tighter monetary policy.

In a recent development, dallas Fed President Lorie Logan proposed stronger tools to keep Treasury markets functioning during a crisis while leaving room for higher interest rates. Her November 13 remarks separate two potential influences on Bitcoin: relief from disrupted funding and pressure from further monetary tightening.

According to recent reports, in the speech, Logan remarked the Treasury market was functioning very well and presented personal recommendations, rather than announcing an intervention or an adopted Federal Open Market Committee program. She said intervention should be reserved for extreme failures in intermediation; high or rapidly rising yields alone would not justify it.

In a recent development, her rate outlook points toward further tightening. In November 10 remarks, Logan described current monetary policy as accommodative and called for at least two further quarter-point increases to make it modestly restrictive. She made the pace conditional on developments. The FOMC's October 28 decision had maintained the target range at 3.75% to 4%; her preferred path is distinct from that committee decision.

Her preferred starting point is lending against Treasury securities. The Fed could supply funding at a rate consistent with its monetary-policy target, supporting financial stability while maintaining the interest-rate stance it considers necessary.

Recent findings suggest that logan also proposed developing central clearing for the Fed's repo lending. Reducing the balance-sheet costs intermediaries incur when passing funding onward could help that money reach the broader market more efficiently during stress.

In a recent development, purchases would serve a different need. When lending cannot resolve dysfunction, buying securities could free space on intermediaries' balance sheets so they can keep trading. But purchases are harder to separate from monetary policy because they can push down term premiums and stimulate the economy.

Sources indicate that logan suggested holding market-function purchases in a separate account and committing to sell the securities as soon as possible. She argued that purchases expected to unwind promptly should have much less effect on term premiums than holdings kept for years. That would limit the unwanted stimulus, rather than guarantee its elimination.

The stUSDT team did not disclose a reason for winding down the RWA protocol but assured holders that all underlying assets remain fully backed.

Real-world asset (RWA) protocol stUSDT has begun winding down operations, nearly three years after reaching a $2.3 billion total value locked (TVL), ending rewards and opening a six-month redemption window for tokenholders.

The team said that interest accrual on stUSDT ended on Saturday, with holders of stUSDT and its wrapped version, wstUSDT, able to redeem through its official portal until May 14, 2027. The team said requests submitted after the deadline will be handled through customer support in monthly batches through August 2027.

The team did not provide a reason for the shutdown but noted all underlying assets remain fully backed. Holders with tokens on exchanges or DeFi platforms must transfer them to personal wallets before redeeming.

Cointelegraph reached out to stUSDT for more information but did not receive a response before publication.

Meanwhile, JustLend DAO mentioned it would phase out supply and borrowing functions for its wstUSDT market as part of the transition.

Released in July 2023 on Tron, stUSDT allowed users to deposit USDT and earn yields from investments in real-world assets, including short-term government bonds. The protocol later expanded to Ethereum.

It has been revealed that according to DefiLlama data, stUSDT’s TVL peaked at about $2.3 billion in November 2023 before declining substantially in subsequent years. It stood at about $8.6 million on Sunday, down from roughly $60 million a year earlier.

Despite its name, stUSDT is not affiliated with stablecoin issuer Tether. In September 2023, Tether denied any affiliation with stUSDT, saying the protocol was an independent project.

Bitcoin price has plunged toward $65,000, raising fresh concerns about whether BTC could crash toward $60,000. The latest sell-off has pushed Bitcoin below $68,000, while ETF outflows and heavy liquidations continue to weaken market demand. With BTC approaching a critical support zone after several consecutive weekly losses, investors are watching for signs of a reversal. Is Bitcoin heading toward $60K, or can buyers stop the decline?

Recent findings suggest that bitcoin’s breakdown below $68,000 has shifted the market’s attention toward lower support levels. The cryptocurrency dropped below $66,000 on November 14, reaching its weakest level since August as selling pressure continued through the weekend.

The decline has also extended Bitcoin’s losing streak, putting it on course for a sixth consecutive weekly loss. From its October highs near $86,000, BTC has now surrendered a substantial portion of its gains.

Macroeconomic concerns are adding to the pressure. Hotter US inflation has strengthened expectations of further Federal Reserve rate increases, while a stronger dollar and rising Treasury yields have reduced appetite for riskier assets. That combination leaves Bitcoin vulnerable as investors reassess their exposure to speculative investments.

Institutional demand is becoming another major concern for Bitcoin investors. US spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded approximately $185.45 million in net outflows on November 13, extending their withdrawal streak to seven consecutive trading sessions.

Sources indicate that the cumulative outflows reached roughly $1.91 billion between November 5 and November 13. BlackRock’s IBIT accounted for a significant portion of the withdrawals, highlighting the scale of institutional selling pressure.

However, the broader ETF picture is not entirely negative. Despite the recent withdrawals, cumulative net inflows across US spot Bitcoin ETFs remained above $54 billion, with total net assets around $86.2 billion.

It has been revealed that the immediate concern is whether persistent redemptions will continue to weaken demand. If ETF withdrawals extend into another week, Bitcoin could struggle to attract enough buying interest to establish a durable recovery.

According to recent reports, bitcoin’s decline has also triggered a major wave of forced selling across the derivatives market. Approximately $1.5 billion in leveraged crypto positions were liquidated over 24 hours, with bullish positions accounting for the overwhelming majority.

Bitcoin positions represented a substantial share of those liquidations. When leveraged long positions are forcibly closed, exchanges sell the underlying exposure, potentially accelerating an existing decline.

In a recent development, this creates additional pressure during periods of weak liquidity. Traders who expected Bitcoin to recover are being forced out of positions, while fresh buyers remain cautious about entering before the market stabilizes.

Bitcoin price is approaching a critical technical zone after losing the $70,000 and $68,000 levels. The price action highlights a sustained downward trend, with lower highs and lower lows indicating that sellers remain in control.

In a recent development, the $64,000–$68,000 region is now an key demand zone. If buyers defend this area and push BTC back above $68,000–$70,000, the cryptocurrency could attempt a short-term recovery. However, a sustained breakdown below $64,000 would expose the next major support near $60,000–$61,000. That level could become the market’s next significant test if selling pressure continues.

Science Prediction Universe found that pooling rankings improved average results, while shared scientific errors survived.

AI models agreed more closely with one another than with laboratory measurements in a new test of AI predictions. Pooling their rankings improved results on average, but several systems could still share the same mistake.

In a recent development, the Science Prediction Universe study, led by UniPat AI and submitted to arXiv on Nov. 11, tested 13 agent configurations spanning 12 models on 100 public tasks and 16 private tasks. Each configuration combined a model, reasoning setting and agent software. The study asked them to rank specified experiments across chemistry, materials science, biology and medicine.

Science Prediction Universe researchers reported that, on the public tasks, average agreement between scored configurations reached a Spearman rank correlation of 0.52, compared with 0.33 against measured outcomes. Agreement between agents exceeded their correlation with measurements on 81 of the 100 tasks. These averages use available scored predictions, with coverage varying by configuration.

Those figures describe how closely orderings match, rather than percentages of answers correct. Agents might rank reaction conditions by yield or materials by conductivity without having to predict numerical values. A perfect ordering without measurement ties scores 1; random rankings average 0.

The researchers found a benefit to pooling predictions. Averaging each experiment's position across configurations produced a consensus ranking that scored 0.08 points above the average submission, improving results on 73 of the 100 public tasks. The reported 95% confidence interval for the gain was 0.05 to 0.11.

On one oncology task, eleven configurations agreed at 0.9 but averaged just 0.27 against measurements. The benchmark’s best individual system also beat the consensus of its peers on matched tasks.

Sources indicate that more broadly, tasks with greater agreement tended to have better predictions. The paper's agreement analysis therefore presents consensus as an informative but fallible signal. The authors explain that averaging can reduce errors that differ between systems while retaining common ones.

#523. Blockstream And Thales Launch Bitcoin Custody System

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4 min read (812 words)
