Blockstream And Thales Launch Bitcoin Custody System

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read | Sumber: https://bitcoinist.com/blockstream-and-thales-launch-bitcoin-custody-system/

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the biggest crypto hack in history started with a fake job interview.
  • Sources indicate that blockstream, the tech giant led by co-founder and CEO Adam Back, has debuted an enterprise custody solution developed with French technology and cybersecurity group Thales, according to a company announcement on Nov.
  • The pitch is straightforward: keep the most sensitive part of moving bitcoin, signing transactions, locked inside dedicated security hardware where hackers cannot reach it.

Recent findings suggest that the biggest crypto hack in history started with a fake job interview. Now one of Bitcoin’s oldest infrastructure firms is betting that the answer to AI-era attacks is simpler, hardware-first Bitcoin custody.

Sources indicate that blockstream, the tech giant led by co-founder and CEO Adam Back, has debuted an enterprise custody solution developed with French technology and cybersecurity group Thales, according to a company announcement on Nov. 13.

The pitch is straightforward: keep the most sensitive part of moving bitcoin, signing transactions, locked inside dedicated security hardware where hackers cannot reach it.

And the timing could not be more relevant.

The solution is delivered through Blockstream Enterprise, the company’s institutional platform, and builds on a two-year relationship between the two firms.

Recent findings suggest that it combines Thales’ hardware security modules (HSMs) with Blockstream’s Secure Multi-Party Computation, or Secure-MPC. MPC spreads signing authority across several parties, so no single person or device controls the private key.

The key difference is where that process happens. Blockstream indicates its system executes the signing protocol entirely within the HSM’s secure environment, while conventional MPC solutions may expose parts of the process to general-purpose computers that are easier to attack.

The system also uses FROST, a threshold signing protocol that lets multiple authorized parties jointly produce a signature without ever reconstructing the full private key.

“By moving MPC execution inside the HSM, this architecture addresses critical security risks,” said Jeff Boortz, Blockstream’s chief product officer.

The launch comes just two weeks after hackers stole about $6.3 billion from Binance, an attack the FBI attributed to North Korea.

Recent findings suggest that the weak point was not the blockchain. It was people and connected computers. Binance said attackers staged fake job interviews and planted malware in a coding assignment downloaded onto an engineer’s work computer.

It has been revealed that AI played a role too. The campaign included a June incident in which a wallet engineer downloaded a tampered installer while looking for an AI coding tool. By Oct. 20, the attackers had used a compromised computer and an internal AI tool to break into the machines of two more employees working on Binance’s wallet infrastructure, according to BleepingComputer, obtaining credentials and a container deployment token.

It has been revealed that that chain of events is exactly what hardware-based Bitcoin custody is designed to stop. If signing keys never leave a sealed device, a hacked laptop is far less useful.

In a recent development, adam Back, the cryptographer whose Hashcash system helped lay the groundwork for Bitcoin’s proof-of-work, has long championed offline key storage. Blockstream already builds hardware wallets and HSMs for cold storage, alongside enterprise wallets for custodians.

Sources indicate that the broader industry is moving in the same direction. Thales has also expanded its work with Fireblocks to keep signing operations inside customer-owned HSMs at banks and regulated institutions.

It has been revealed that the idea is simple. As AI makes it easier for attackers to find small mistakes in complex software, the safest approach is to cut down the number of places where keys can be exposed.

Blockstream knows the stakes firsthand. In September, its Liquid Network sidechain was drained of nearly 4,000 BTC through a software bug, with the attackers returning 3,400 BTC after the flaw was patched.

For institutions, security is the gatekeeper. Banks and asset managers cannot hold bitcoin at scale without custody that meets the same standards as the rest of their operations.

“Financial institutions require secure, reliable infrastructure as they integrate bitcoin into their existing operations,” stated Michael Minkevich, Blockstream’s president and chief operating officer.

Recent findings suggest that that demand has been building since spot Bitcoin ETFs became top performers after their 2024 launch, pulling Wall Street deeper into the asset. Stronger custody options make it easier for the next wave of institutions to follow.

Recent findings suggest that the market itself is under pressure, with Bitcoin trading below $70,000 after a sharp sell-off. But behind the price, the infrastructure that will hold the next trillion dollars of bitcoin keeps getting stronger. For more updates, follow the latest Bitcoin news.

Will the Binance hack push more institutions toward hardware-based Bitcoin custody, or is self-custody in cold storage still the only real answer?

Cardano founder Charles Hoskinson is sending out a hopeful message to the crypto space in the wake of a brutal market crash that is causing ADA to come very close to falling out of the top 20 crypto assets.

Recently, Hoskinson took to X to respond to a frustrated Cardano fan who posted a screenshot showing ADA falling almost 10% in the last 24 hours.

“It’s all going to be ok,” said Hoskinson. “Everyone will be happy next year after all this madness, hate and idiocy.”.

The recent crypto market crash has proven to be extremely brutal for a lot of different assets, and Cardano is certainly one of the worst affected.

In recent trading, ADA has fallen all the way down to around $0.15.

At these levels, ADA is currently down around 95% from its all-time high of $3.09, which was reached in September 2021, based on data from CoinGecko.

This represents an almost complete loss of investment value for those who bought at the all-time high.

Overall, Cardano is also down around 35% in the last month and almost 60% since the start of 2026.

As a result, Cardano’s market cap has fallen all the way down to around $5.7 billion, with ADA dropping to 18th place in CoinGecko’s crypto rankings.

This is a very precarious position for the once-dominant altcoin Cardano, which is now extremely close to falling out of the top 20.

It seems as though there are a few different factors at play behind Cardano’s poor performance.

In a recent development, first of all, there has been a huge sell-off in the broader crypto market. Bitcoin has seen major drops, leading to more selling pressure on major altcoins.

This decline has coincided with a falling technology stock market, ongoing macroeconomic uncertainty, outflows from crypto investment products, and mass liquidations of leveraged positions.

That stated, there are clearly some challenges with Cardano beyond the wider market struggles.

Industry observers note that for one, Cardano has faced a lot of criticism over the years for the blockchain’s relatively low adoption, even after years of development. This is especially evident when compared to other chains like Ethereum and Solana.

In fact, Cardano’s decentralized finance ecosystem has recently seen around $46 million in total value locked, as reported by DefiLlama.

Elsewhere, Hoskinson recently found himself embroiled in another controversy surrounding Cardano’s future.

In another recent X post, Hoskinson lashed out at certain commentators who keep bashing the blockchain for its apparent lack of adoption.

He noted that critics initially claimed Cardano suffered from poor on-chain metrics, few real-world use cases and technology that no one wanted to use.

Then, when Hoskinson decided to work on developing apps that would be able to attract millions of people and billions in assets, it seemed as though those same critics began claiming he was scamming everyone.

It has been revealed that “You people are both stupid and scum. I can’t fix stupid,” said Hoskinson. “Grow up.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, bitcoin is bleeding ahead of the biggest AI listing in history.
  • BTC dropped below $67,000 this week, its weakest level since August, as investors pulled money from spot ETFs ahead of the Anthropic IPO.
  • In a recent development, the massive question on crypto is simple: are whales selling bitcoin to buy into the Anthropic IPO?

According to recent reports, bitcoin is bleeding ahead of the biggest AI listing in history. But if the market follows the script it wrote just five months ago, the selling could soon run out of fuel.

BTC dropped below $67,000 this week, its weakest level since August, as investors pulled money from spot ETFs ahead of the Anthropic IPO. Anthropic is set to price its shares on Nov. 18 and begin trading on Nasdaq on Nov. 19.

In a recent development, the massive question on crypto is simple: are whales selling bitcoin to buy into the Anthropic IPO? The data offers some clues.

Sources indicate that according to figures circulating widely on X, about $2.35 billion has flowed out of US spot Bitcoin ETFs over the past two weeks. BlackRock’s IBIT has led the exodus with 11 straight sessions of redemptions, accounting for roughly 90% of November’s outflows.

Macro pressure is adding to the strain. Fed Governor Christopher Waller’s support for a December rate hike pushed CME FedWatch odds of such a move to 96.3%, while a tech sell-off has weighed on all risk assets. Bitcoin crashed below $70,000 earlier this week as liquidations topped $1.6 billion.

This has happened before. In the run-up to SpaceX’s record $75 billion IPO in June, Bitcoin went through an almost identical cycle:.

The bottom is well documented. Bitcoin touched as low as $59,375 on June 5, as data showed at the time. Standard Chartered’s Geoffrey Kendrick then called the cycle low, arguing that heavy selling of spot Bitcoin ETFs, partly to free cash for SpaceX’s IPO, was likely to ease once the listing began.

Sources indicate that the scale of that drain was large. More than $5.72 billion of spot Bitcoin ETF redemptions since mid-May were tied to investors freeing capital for the SpaceX offering.

It has been revealed that crypto analyst Benjamin Cowen took the comparison a step further. In a post on X, e overlaid Bitcoin’s price in the 30 days before and after the SpaceX IPO with its performance in the roughly 30 days leading up to the Anthropic listing.

The two lines move almost in lockstep through the start of the window, each slipping a few percent in the first week.

The SpaceX path also offers a lesson in patience. In Cowen’s chart, Bitcoin was down about 20% by SpaceX’s listing day and dipped to roughly 25% below its starting point in the weeks after, before stabilizing. The real recovery came later, once the IPO selling pressure had fully cleared.

In a recent development, if the pattern holds, more selling could happen around Nov. 19. But it would also suggest the market is in the late stages of the drawdown, not the beginning.

There are two reasons the selling pressure could be lighter this time.

First, the retail slice is smaller. Anthropic expects to allocate up to 20% of its IPO shares to retail investors, about $11.55 billion to $12.87 billion at its price range, according to FourWeekMBA’s analysis of the organization’s amended prospectus. SpaceX initially planned to give retail around 30% of a much larger $75 billion deal, before trimming it to the low 20% range.

A smaller retail pool means less cash that needs to be raised, potentially by selling crypto.

Recent findings suggest that second, Anthropic’s separate $26 billion private placement is being funded by its own compute suppliers, including Nvidia, Google and Microsoft. That money comes from corporate balance sheets, not the same pool of investor cash that might otherwise sit in bitcoin.

The first level for bulls is $70,000. Reclaiming it would show buyers stepping back in after a sharp week.

Above that, the $76,000 zone is the next key hurdle, followed by the $80,000 to $82,000 resistance range.

According to recent reports, on the downside, this week’s low near $67,000 is the line to hold. A break below it could open a move toward the $59,000 to $60,000 area, the same zone where Bitcoin bottomed before the SpaceX listing.

According to recent reports, still, the IPO is not the only driver. If the Fed’s rate decision and the tech sell-off keep pushing investors out of risk, the end of IPO selling alone won’t be enough to turn Bitcoin around. For more updates, follow the latest Bitcoin news.

Tech Report: Newly introduced Monero Privacy Update Might Be Coming Soon: Key Improvement

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read | Sumber: https://u.today/new-monero-privacy-update-might-be-coming-soon-key-improvement

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today.
  • Monero contributor has opened a pull request that changes how nodes relay transactions coming from Tor and I2P, according to the project's GitHub.
  • The patch addresses a privacy weakness that could allow an observer to connect a transaction to the anonymity network it came from due to the timing of its broadcast.

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

Monero contributor has opened a pull request that changes how nodes relay transactions coming from Tor and I2P, according to the project's GitHub.

The patch addresses a privacy weakness that could allow an observer to connect a transaction to the anonymity network it came from due to the timing of its broadcast.

PR 11743 was opened on November 13 and is right now pending review. It is an updated version of a PR opened on November 8 by contributor vtnerd. After receiving feedback from another Monero developer, vtnerd, the PR was updated.

The glitch lies in a mechanism where a node receives a transaction over Tor or I2P and then passes it to the regular Monero network.

At the moment, when a Monero node receives a transaction over Tor or I2P, it relays that transaction to the rest of the Monero network.

It has been revealed that while the transaction is technically private as it travels into the node, once it reaches Monero's public peers, the transaction is no longer private. This PR proposes that Monero nodes will only accept transactions from Tor and I2P peers over incoming connections. Transactions received over outgoing Tor and I2P connections would be ignored.

Sources indicate that once accepted, the transaction would be subject to a random delay before being relayed to the rest of the Monero network using Monero's existing transaction relay protocol, Dandelion++. Presently, a user can instruct their node to broadcast their transaction immediately.

Over Tor and I2P connections, this request would be ignored. No transaction would be exempt from the random delay.Being able to link a transaction's timing between the anonymity network and the Monero network is an easy way to deanonymize a user. If a transaction is broadcast to the Monero network immediately after being received from Tor, an observer watching both networks can link the two.

This is a similar concept to a previous PR from vtnerd that would have introduced a randomized delay when relaying transactions from Tor and I2P to the Monero network.

While the amount of code that would need to be modified is not particularly large, this does close a hole for users that rely on Tor and I2P to obscure their location.

Sources indicate that when the patch lands in a release is yet to be confirmed. The PR is also labeled for a backport, so it might reach the current release branch as well.

Firstly, Lee points out that the recent crash in AI and semiconductor stocks, especially Nvidia, may have led to margin calls, particularly for retail investors in Asian markets.

Solana’s biggest week of the year got off to a painful start. But beneath the price chart, Solana staking tells a very different story.

It has been revealed that SOL fell as low as $67.37 overnight into Sunday, its lowest level since late June. The drop landed on the very first day of Breakpoint, the Solana Foundation’s flagship conference, held in London for the first time from Nov. 15 to 17.

Sources indicate that the token is now trading near $70, down about 6.8% in 24 hours and more than 20% below where it stood on Nov. 4.

Yet roughly two-thirds of all SOL remains locked up in staking, and holders show little sign of rushing for the exits.

It has been revealed that the sell-off has little to do with Solana itself. It is being driven by the same macro pressure hitting the entire crypto market.

Industry observers note that fed Governor Christopher Waller’s support for a December rate hike pushed CME FedWatch odds of such a move to 96.3%, per BigGo Finance. The crypto Fear and Greed Index has sunk to 13, deep in extreme fear territory, while Bitcoin has dropped below $70,000.

Institutional demand has also cooled. US spot Solana ETFs have now posted seven straight days of outflows totaling around $58.3 million, a sharp contrast to earlier this year, when Solana ETF inflows topped $1.16 billion.

Recent findings suggest that leverage did the rest. Around $67 million in long positions were liquidated as SOL broke through support, forcing more selling into a falling market.

Here is where the picture changes. As of Nov. 8, 434.15 million SOL was staked with voting validators, or 68.14% of the total supply, according to Cryptoticker’s analysis.

Recent findings suggest that bitwise’s latest staking report found that Solana ended the third quarter with 69% of its supply staked, the highest of the six networks it tracks. By comparison, Ethereum stood at 33%.

On Solana, staking has become the default. Holding unstaked SOL is the exception, not the rule.

According to recent reports, stakers are earning a gross yield of about 5.2%, or close to 5% after a typical validator commission. High participation strengthens network security and keeps a large share of supply off the market, which helps limit the pool of coins available to sell during panics like this one.

The ratio has slipped slightly in recent weeks, with around 4.8 million SOL leaving active staking over 30 days. But with nearly 70% of supply still committed, the core holder base remains firmly in place.

The timing of the crash is awkward, but it also puts the spotlight on what comes next. More than 8,000 attendees are expected at London’s Olympia this week, with sessions focused on stablecoins, onchain capital markets and AI agents.

Development has not slowed down either. Arcium recently opened Blackthorn, a private AI inference stack built for Solana that runs AI models with prompts, outputs and model weights encrypted. That builds on October’s Alpenglow upgrade, which cut finality to around 150 milliseconds.

It has been revealed that past conferences show the price reaction can vary. At Breakpoint 2023 in Amsterdam, SOL rallied 20% during the event and kept climbing for weeks. In Abu Dhabi last year, the price slipped 2.3% during the conference before recovering over the following month.

According to recent reports, the first line to hold is the overnight low near $67.40. Holding above it would suggest sellers are running out of steam after a brutal week.

Industry observers note that on the upside, SOL needs to reclaim the August level around $71.90 first, then the $75 to $80 zone it lost over the past two days. A move back above $80 would put SOL back in the range it held before its earlier slide below that level.

The bigger target is the 200-day moving average, just under $89. Reclaiming that line would mark a clear trend shift.

If $67 fails, the psychological $60 level becomes the next major support.

For now, Solana staking data reveals that most holders are choosing to stay put and earn yield rather than sell into the panic. For more updates, follow the latest altcoin news.

Can Breakpoint spark a SOL recovery this week, or does the price need to retest $60 before Solana’s strong staking base pays off?

#534. Breaking: AI Cyberattacks And Outages Keep Breaking Centralized Systems, But Bitcoin Keeps Running

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4 min read (822 words)

Breaking: AI Cyberattacks And Outages Keep Breaking Centralized Systems, But Bitcoin Keeps Running

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read | Sumber: https://bitcoinist.com/ai-cyberattacks-outages-keep-breaking-centralized-systems-but-bitcoin-keeps-running/

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, AI cyberattacks and outages have made the past few months brutal for the systems the modern internet runs on.
  • Yet through all of it, one network never missed a beat.
  • Sources indicate that the Bitcoin blockchain has been running continuously since 2009 and has never been breached.

According to recent reports, AI cyberattacks and outages have made the past few months brutal for the systems the modern internet runs on. Cloud platforms have gone dark, AI tools have failed in waves, and hackers have pulled off the biggest heist in history.

Yet through all of it, one network never missed a beat.

Sources indicate that the Bitcoin blockchain has been running continuously since 2009 and has never been breached. As AI makes attacks faster and outages more disruptive, that track record is becoming one of crypto’s strongest selling points.

It has been revealed that the latest disruption started on Nov. 12, when a Microsoft outage centered on Exchange Online knocked out Outlook, Teams, SharePoint and Copilot. By its second day, it had also broken the Microsoft 365 connectors inside ChatGPT and Claude, cutting both AI assistants off from owners’ work email, calendars and documents.

On Nov. 13, Anthropic also opened a separate incident as consumers struggled to log in to Claude.ai and Claude Code. Neither organization has linked the problems to an attack.

It has been revealed that it was not the first time. On Sept. 3, ChatGPT, Claude and Grok went down at roughly the same time. xAI blamed an outage at its Memphis data center, but the timing set off speculation. Cardano founder Charles Hoskinson suggested a nation state may have been behind it, a theory that remains unconfirmed.

The outages came alongside a wave of real attacks. Security firm Wiz dubbed last month “Black October” after counting at least nine AI development platforms that disclosed security incidents.

According to recent reports, many of those attacks aimed to steal API keys for AI models, and in some cases researchers suspected AI “agent swarms” were doing the work. AI is now both a target and a weapon.

Crypto has already felt the impact. In August, Bitcoin swap protocol Boltz suspended its services after attackers used AI to probe and exploit vulnerabilities faster than the team could patch them.

Coinbase’s chief security officer Philip Martin has warned that advanced AI models “will accelerate digital threats as well as digital defense.”.

Then came the biggest one of all. On Oct. 29, hackers stole about $6.3 billion from Binance’s hot wallets, the largest crypto theft on record. The FBI attributed it to North Korea’s TraderTraitor unit, the same group behind the $1.5 billion Bybit hack in 2025.

Investigators traced the entry point to a compromised employee laptop. In other words, the weak spot was a centralized company’s internal systems, not the blockchains themselves.

Industry observers note that the response highlighted the industry’s resilience. Binance stated it replenished around 90% of the stolen assets within days, and stablecoin issuers froze more than $2.4 billion of the stolen funds.

Notably, when Binance began reopening withdrawals, the first network it switched back on was Bitcoin.

Recent findings suggest that there is a clear pattern here. Every major failure, from Microsoft’s cloud to AI chatbots to Binance’s hot wallets, happened at a single point of control. When that one point breaks, everything built on it goes down.

Sources indicate that bitcoin is built the opposite way. Thousands of independent nodes around the world keep the network running, so there is no single server to take offline and no single company to hack.

That is why every substantial outage revives the case for decentralized infrastructure. It is also why the network is finding latest roles in the AI economy. Lightning Labs just released payments for autonomous AI agents, letting software pay for computing directly in bitcoin.

According to recent reports, the lesson for investors is straightforward. The risk lives at the edges: exchanges, custodians, wallets and the cloud services they rely on. Holding coins in self-custody and choosing platforms with strong security practices matter more than ever in an age of AI-powered attacks.

Sources indicate that the hacks have weighed on sentiment. Bitcoin fell nearly 5% after the Binance theft, and it has since dropped below $70,000 amid a broader risk-off move.

But the network itself has not wavered. Blocks keep coming, transactions keep settling, and the protocol keeps working, whether ChatGPT is online or not. For more updates, follow the latest Bitcoin news.

Will AI-powered cyberattacks push more people toward decentralized networks like Bitcoin, or will they make crypto platforms an even bigger target?

#537. Latest Update: Binance Warns About AI Scams

Latest Update: Binance Warns About AI Scams

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read | Sumber: https://u.today/binance-warns-about-ai-scams

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Cryptocurrency exchange Binance has warned of the rising risk of AI scams, including the use of deepfakes that impersonate Binance executives and staff.
  • The world's largest crypto exchange recently took to X to warn its users that improvements in artificial intelligence are making it harder to distinguish fake messages from real ones.
  • "AI deepfakes are making impersonation scams harder to spot," the crypto exchange remarked in a post.

Cryptocurrency exchange Binance has warned of the rising risk of AI scams, including the use of deepfakes that impersonate Binance executives and staff.

The world's largest crypto exchange recently took to X to warn its users that improvements in artificial intelligence are making it harder to distinguish fake messages from real ones.

"AI deepfakes are making impersonation scams harder to spot," the crypto exchange remarked in a post.

The cryptocurrency exchange has assured its users that no one from Binance will ever reach out to them asking for money or offering unsolicited investment advice.

Binance says scammers are making realistic deepfake videos featuring executives and employees of the manufacturer.

Fraudsters are using these deepfakes, some of which are very realistic, to trick potential targets through fraudulent video calls.

That way, people who fall victim to the scam might think they are interacting with real Binance personnel.

Sources indicate that binance warned that scammers often try to reach potential targets through messaging apps such as WhatsApp or Telegram. They impersonate Binance employees by using their names, photos, and job titles to appear credible.

After making contact with a potential victim, the scammer may try to convince them to send crypto, take part in an exclusive investment opportunity, or take other financial actions.

Binance has called on crypto consumers to be cautious about any unexpected messages they receive, even if they seem to be from someone at the company they know.

A realistic appearance no longer guarantees a person's identity, given that AI can now easily mimic voices and facial expressions.

Users should double-check any suspicious messages through official Binance support channels before taking any action.

#539. Tech Report: Enterprise blockchain is going to come back from the dead

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7 min read (1313 words)
General

Tech Report: Enterprise blockchain is going to come back from the dead

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read | Sumber: https://cointelegraph.com/opinion/enterprise-blockchain-come-back-from-dead?utm_source=rss_feed&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=rss_partner_inbound

💡 Key Takeaways
  • With scalability, privacy tools and onchain liquidity improving, businesses may finally have the infrastructure to make enterprise blockchain work.
  • Opinion by Paul Brody, founder and chief executive, Nightfall Networks.
  • According to recent reports, do you remember Pets.com?

With scalability, privacy tools and onchain liquidity improving, businesses may finally have the infrastructure to make enterprise blockchain work.

Opinion by Paul Brody, founder and chief executive, Nightfall Networks.

According to recent reports, do you remember Pets.com? It raised $110 million from Amazon and others to build a business where people ordered pet toys and dog food online.

The tech giant crashed and burned, and everyone learned an notable lesson: you can’t profitably ship a 50-pound bag of dog food to a customer’s door.

As online retail entrepreneur Ed Baum asked in a 2001 postmortem: “Did Pets.com’s business initiative assume the invention of transporters to magically move bags of pet food without shipping costs?”.

Sources indicate that please, whatever you do, don’t share this with the people at Chewy; they might not realize their business model doesn’t work. Chewy reported $12.6 billion in sales and $223 million in net income in its latest fiscal year.

The real lesson of Pets.com wasn’t that shipping dog food was a bad idea. It’s that the idea arrived before the logistics, customer habits and unit economics required to make it work.

As it was with chew toys and dog food, so it may be with enterprise blockchains.

According to recent reports, collectively, the crypto industry probably incinerated just as much money trying that between 2017 and 2023 as Pets.com. Maybe more. But the dozens of companies that went after enterprise blockchain were not delusional; they were just too early.

It’s not hard to understand the appeal of enterprise blockchain solutions, at least superficially. Nearly all enterprise systems today tend to fail at the boundaries between companies. There are two failure modes: mode 1, the OG failure mode, where collaboration information is constantly out of sync.

In this world, enterprise IT systems are islands, communicating asynchronously with each other by digital text messages and emailed spreadsheets. It’s cheap and easy to set up, if you don’t mind always having slightly wrong information.

Related: Privacy is missing ingredient for business blockchain adoption: EY exec.

Industry observers note that failure mode two is the costly, real-time proprietary integration. Powerful industry leaders politely request their key suppliers and partners to join their closed but always-on networks.

Chewy reported $223 million in net income in its latest fiscal year. Source: Chewy.

These are very costly, but they work well and leave everyone with a kind of business version of Stockholm syndrome, where you come to appreciate the thoroughness and efficiency of the digital choke-hold you are in.

In a recent development, blockchains offered a better path forward: shared information and business logic across an open ecosystem. All the benefits of a proprietary system in terms of real-time visibility and efficiency, without the lock-in.

Sometime around 2017, this started to look like a very obvious good idea. Investment poured in, consortia introduced, press releases were drafted and released, and then pretty much everything crashed and burned. TradeLens, We.Trade, Contour, B3i, ASX Chess, Everledger. All came and went in just a few years.

Though there is a lot of nuance to the details of each of these stories, they all largely have one thing in common: they had to do unnatural things to make up for the lack of privacy available natively in blockchains.

Industry observers note that no firm wants their competition to see what they’re doing in detail. Mostly, this meant building a private/permissioned chain and then doing lots of non-blockchain-like things to it and in it to try to keep information private. The results were uniformly slow and expensive and failed to gain traction.

Recent findings suggest that it’s hard to understate the bloodbath of companies and startups that tried and failed to make enterprise blockchain work. A quick web and history search turned up 18 different ones, some of them well-known.

Industry observers note that many had big-name backers, from major banks like Deutsche Bank and HSBC to technology companies like IBM. Pedigreed parents and big brands made no difference — privacy didn’t work and the results were dismal.

According to recent reports, what few survivors of this are left have “de-chained” themselves — giving up the blockchain theater and reverting to a classic software-as-a-service (SaaS) model. Many companies that tried and tested these permissioned enterprise systems as users came away from their experience with a clear learning: we tried blockchain, it didn’t work.

That’s unfortunate because everything is different now.

Blockchains have scale. Ethereum in 2020 handled 1 million transactions a day and costs per transaction periodically spiked to $30-50 when demand was high. Today, most transactions get done under a penny and capacity is ramping toward billions of transactions a day. Nobody talks about the “trilemma” anymore. Ethereum is decentralized and it is scaled.

Related: Ethereum’s Glamsterdam upgrade launches on Sepolia testnet.

Sources indicate that privacy is different now, too. While privacy is still not the default setting, a huge range of privacy tools and systems are now available, from privacy pools to zero-knowledge roll-ups and full privacy chains.

On top of that, Ethereum is building a range of tools that will add basic elements of privacy at multiple levels in the network. The result: it’s now possible to run business operations at scale with a high degree of privacy.

Finally, there’s the money. It’s all moving onchain. Regulators around the globe have blessed stablecoins and the result is a tsunami of liquidity, with transaction volume reaching almost $1.8 trillion in June.

If we combine the operational benefits of blockchains with the financial ones, we get something that enterprises have never really had before: a single ecosystem where you can not only buy, sell, and move assets, but get paid for them as well.

There was just under $1.8 trillion in adjusted stablecoin transaction volume in June. Source: Visa.

In a recent development, the return on investment from every single component of this equation is massive. Combined, they can yield colossal advantages. McKinsey partners even found that digital supply chain tools could make inventory reductions of 35-75% possible through better planning.

According to recent reports, more conservatively, from my experience in the field, just switching away from the existing cascades of spreadsheets and electronic data interchange (EDI) messages can allow firms to run most supply chains with about 20% less inventory at the same service level. That’s worth billions in working capital in most industries.

Recent findings suggest that it gets better from there. Smart contracts reduce the time required to handle many business contract rules from days to minutes and cut the costs of administration in half.

Microsoft began moving its Xbox video game network onto smart contracts for handling royalties and cut the time to access monthly royalty statements from 45 days to four minutes. All that while handling more than 2 million transactions a day.

And once you have inventories, contracts, purchase orders and invoices onchain, you can go after working capital directly as well.

When you can prove your purchase order originates from a top-quality buyer, you can access credit for less. And when you have full visibility into inventory and delivery status, you can factor receivables immediately and efficiently.

It has been revealed that the possibilities and the returns are big. The use cases are obvious. It’s time to try again.

How Wall Street Is Racing to Claim the Onchain Dollar

How Wall Street Is Racing to Claim the Onchain Dollar.

For years, stablecoins were crypto’s business, dominated by Tether and Circle and used mostly to trade digital assets. That era is ending.

Over the past few months, and especially the past few weeks, the biggest names in traditional finance have moved en masse to claim a piece of the onchain dollar. Here’s the map of a land grab that’s accelerating fast.

The clearest signal came this week, when Goldman Sachs, Citigroup, Santander, and Deutsche Bank were reported to be among banks committing roughly $270 million to a joint dollar-stablecoin venture codenamed “Project Faro.”.

Sources indicate that the capital funds five years of operations for a U.S.-incorporated issuer targeting a 2027 launch, part of a 21-institution coalition that has swelled from an initial group of 10. The goal is explicit: challenge Tether and Circle, which together still control about 85% of a roughly $290 billion market.

Recent findings suggest that while the consortium prepares, SoFi has shipped. Earlier this week, its SoFiUSD, billed as the first stablecoin from a U.S. national bank, expanded onto Polygon this month alongside Ethereum and Solana, reaching the bank’s 17 million-plus members.

SoFi also introduced SoFi Earn, a tokenized deposit paying 4.40% yield that converts into SoFiUSD, and already settles its entire card program over Mastercard’s network.

Meanwhile, the federally chartered crypto bank Anchorage Digital has positioned itself as a settlement backbone.

Anchorage’s tokens can now settle transactions on Visa’s network, starting with Western Union’s USDPT, and it recently anchored both sides of the U.S.-Mexico stablecoin corridor, custodying tokens across one of the world’s largest remittance routes.

Mastercard has been the most aggressive incumbent among payment giants.

It rolled out a Global Money Platform with acquired stablecoin firm BVNK, rolled out a Stablecoin Security tool to screen payments for fraud, and unveiled Agent Pay for Machines, letting AI agents transact in stablecoins.

Visa, meanwhile, has expanded its own stablecoin settlement program across multiple blockchains.

The crypto-native incumbents, not to be left out, are also racing to entrench.

Circle struck a deal to bring USDC settlement to banking rails in Latin America, starting with a Colombia pilot, part of a broader expansion into dozens of emerging markets.

In a recent development, the catalyst is regulation. The GENIUS Act, signed in 2025, created the first U.S. framework for dollar-pegged tokens, giving regulated institutions a clear path into a business they had largely watched from the sidelines.

The Donald Trump administration has framed dollar stablecoins as a tool to extend the dollar’s reach and global hegemony, and banks that once dismissed crypto now see a settlement business they can’t afford to cede.

It has been revealed that much of this remains early. Project Faro has no token, no CEO, and no final name. Tether and Circle still dominate, and bank-issued tokens face a steep climb to win share.

But the direction is unmistakable: the onchain dollar, once crypto’s turf, is now contested ground, with Wall Street, the card networks and the stablecoin incumbents all racing to own the rails money moves on.

It has been revealed that according to Fang, XRPL had almost no transactions made by AI agents three or four months before the interview, which was recorded at XRP Seoul 2026. "The entire volume got ramped up very swiftly in the three months," he remarked.

According to recent reports, the x402 Facilitator works as a bridge between AI agents and payments, and agents can use XRP or the RLUSD stablecoin to move money without a separate wallet setup for every agent. Fang said that more than 200 merchants are already on the network.

Recent findings suggest that according to Fang, the most common use case is paying for AI compute. Instead of paying $20 to $200 a month for an AI subscription, an agent can pay around $1 or 50 cents for a single task. "Instead, they can purchase this single compute for about $1, or 50 cents, and it can be settled on the XRPL," Fang remarked.

Recent findings suggest that fang said that such payments have low value and high frequency, so the high throughput and low fees of XRPL give the network an advantage. He also expects agent payments to move into real-life purchases over the next few quarters. "We have the coffee shop right outside our booth, right? And we are trying to empower owners to use XRP and agent payments to finish a real-life transaction," Fang said.

According to recent reports, according to Fang, trust is the main matter for agent payments, and t54.ai's Trustline product focuses on risk management for the financial activity of AI agents. He compared the service with the chargeback feature of credit cards. "So there is no lawsuit. It is a similar experience for agents," Fang mentioned.

It has been revealed that t54.ai is also part of Mastercard's agentic payment program, where the startup is responsible for risk management. The x402 Facilitator processes transactions based on Mastercard Verifiable Intent, a protocol that verifies the behavior of AI agents.

Fang said that t54.ai, Ripple and Mastercard are in talks about a three-way collaboration, and the first results will be shown at an upcoming hackathon.

Bitcoin ETFs Lose $2.1 Billion in November as Outflow Streak Hits Seven Days.

Bitcoin ETF investors are still heading for the exits, and the price slide is speeding up.

U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs shed $185.4 million on Friday, according to Decrypt’s ETF tracker, extending their outflow streak to seven straight trading days.

The funds lost about $829 million this week after shedding nearly $1.3 billion the week before, bringing November’s outflows to roughly $2.1 billion.

Recent findings suggest that the selling so far this month has been relentless. The funds bled $1.4 billion over five sessions earlier in the streak as investors cut risk. Cumulative net inflows since launch have slipped to $55.3 billion, and total net assets fell to $94.9 billion, below the $100 billion mark they held through much of October.

Other crypto funds haven’t escaped the rout. Ethereum ETFs took in a modest $2.3 million on Friday, snapping a six-day outflow streak, but still lost about $336 million on the week and roughly $702 million so far in November. Solana ETFs shed about $28 million this week, though they retain $1.6 billion in cumulative net inflows.

Industry observers note that spot crypto ETFs hold the underlying asset, such as Bitcoin or Ethereum, and trade on stock exchanges like ordinary shares, giving investors exposure through a regular brokerage account. Bitcoin funds have drawn $55.3 billion in net inflows since debuting in January 2024. Because issuers report flows daily and much of the money comes from institutions and financial advisers, the figures have become a closely watched gauge of investor sentiment.

The outflows have tracked a sharp sell-off. Bitcoin traded near $64,500 over the weekend, down 6% over 24 hours and about 15% on the week, according to CoinGecko, and it has lost more than 22% over the past month.

According to recent reports, ethereum fell 8.4% to about $1,790, and Solana dropped 12% to roughly $70. Total crypto market value slid 4.5% to about $2.3 trillion.

Bitcoin hit a 12-week low this week as fears of further Federal Reserve rate hikes erased its summer rally, and concentrated liquidations pushed the price below $69,000 earlier in the week.

Not every institution is retreating. JPMorgan’s holdings of Bitcoin and crypto-linked securities are approaching $1 billion, according to its most recent SEC filing. However, those purchases predate the more recent market downturn.

Sources indicate that an exploit at Kava Lend has drained roughly 55 million KAVA tokens from the lending protocol, highlighting a class of DeFi vulnerability that can remain dormant until unusual market conditions make it dangerous. The incident did not involve an attacker magically creating unlimited tokens. Instead, on-chain analysis indicates that a tiny balance in a largely inactive stablecoin market caused the protocol to overstate the value of collateral, opening the door to repeated borrowing.

The attack and the sharp fall in KAVA's price unfolded on November 14. The protocol team has remarked the incident was contained within Kava Lend, but a full official post-mortem and recovery strategy had not been published in the reporting reviewed for this article.

Recent findings suggest that according to The Block's account of the incident, the attacker targeted a Kava Lend market for BUSD, a stablecoin whose issuer stopped minting new tokens in 2023. The market was barely active. By pushing its effective net supply extremely close to zero, the attacker triggered a calculation that exaggerated the accounting value of deposits by approximately 243,000 times.

Sources indicate that this was not a huge cash deposit suddenly becoming a huge amount of real money. It was a software-accounting error: the lending system treated collateral as far more valuable than it actually was. Such errors are particularly dangerous in lending protocols because borrowing limits depend on accurate collateral valuations. If that relationship breaks, the system can approve loans that no legitimate market price would support.

In a recent development, the attacker reportedly executed 127 KAVA borrow transactions, drawing roughly 55.2 million tokens from the pool. At the price before the attack, those tokens were worth approximately $3.76 million. Around 49.2 million KAVA were then sent to BNB Chain through LayerZero, with sales producing about $2.09 million in BNB and USDT, according to the published on-chain analysis.

Those figures describe different things. The larger dollar value is an estimate based on the pre-attack token price, while the smaller amount describes proceeds realised after heavy selling into a falling market. The amount borrowed, value lost by lenders and value ultimately recoverable may differ. A definitive accounting should await the protocol's incident report.

Industry observers note that kava mentioned the event was not an infinite-mint problem and was isolated to Kava Lend. It also reported precautionary steps affecting bridging, while some trading venues restricted KAVA transfers. Those actions may limit additional damage, but they do not automatically replenish tokens owed to depositors or explain how the accounting failure escaped detection.

Industry observers note that the most useful follow-up is not a dramatic price prediction. It is a clear statement about who bore the loss, whether any market remains impaired, what code changes are proposed and whether those changes have undergone independent review. The availability of an audit label alone cannot substitute for understanding the exact edge case that failed.

Recent findings suggest that lending protocols routinely make complex decisions using collateral ratios, interest indexes, liquidity pools and oracle prices. As NewsBTC's coverage of Aave governance demonstrates, even mature money markets require ongoing decisions about risk and economic design. Institutional interest in lending infrastructure makes those controls more consequential, not less.

The Kava case is a reminder that the most damaging exploit may come from an apparently forgotten market rather than a heavily traded one. For anyone depositing into a DeFi lender, exposure to every supported collateral market can matter, even if they never personally touch the asset that starts the chain reaction.

Banxa’s Shaun Heng Warns Rapid Fintech Growth Can Conceal Hidden Risks

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read | Sumber: https://dailycoin.com/banxas-shaun-heng-warns-rapid-fintech-growth-can-conceal-hidden-risks/

💡 Key Takeaways

Home » Interviews » Banxa’s Shaun Heng Warns Rapid Fintech Growth Can Conceal Hidden Risks.

An interview with Banxa’s Chief Product & Growth Officer on hidden scaling traps and the future of stablecoin payments.

According to recent reports, rapid growth is often seen as a sign of success in fintech. But as transaction volumes increase, weaknesses in payment infrastructure, fraud prevention and risk management can become harder to spot – and more costly to fix.

In a recent development, shaun Heng, Chief Product & Growth Officer at Banxa, a global crypto payments infrastructure provider, knows these challenges firsthand. Before joining Banxa, Heng held product and growth leadership roles at MoonPay and CoinMarketCap, gaining experience across two major players in the digital asset space.

In this interview with DailyCoin, he discusses why rapid growth can expose hidden vulnerabilities in fintech, what it takes to build payment infrastructure that works at scale, and how stablecoins could reshape the future of global payments.

– When does rapid growth become a risk for fintech companies?

Our total transaction volume (TTV) grew 76% from January to August. Stablecoins increased by 117%. Great numbers. The first thing I asked was where they came from?

In a recent development, growth becomes a risk signal the moment it outruns the systems underneath it. That happens more often than people admit.

When volume doubles, every weakness doubles with it. That could mean fraud attempts, chargeback exposure, reconciliation breaks. Just to name a few. So you’re always looking at a great number next to problems that may not have appeared yet.

Recent findings suggest that the second challenge is that fast growth is almost never evenly distributed. It could be one particular partner, region, digital asset, or payment method. That concentration is invisible on a topline chart, so we always look deeper to understand the drivers and future success.

Industry observers note that and team culture is real. In a quarter everyone has worked so hard and exceeded targets, nobody wants to be the one asking hard questions.

The discipline I would push for is simple: break down the growth before you celebrate it. Where is it coming from? Which rails is it riding on? And what happens if one of those rails is withdrawn next week?

Growth becomes a risk signal the moment it outruns the systems underneath it.

– What does a payment infrastructure provider need to deliver to make the crypto on-ramp experience seamless?

For a long time the industry shipped widgets, and a widget is a visible admission that someone else is handling this.

Banxa Native is headless by design. The partner owns the interface, the brand, the pricing presentation, the whole journey. We simply sit behind their stack. Users never.

Sources indicate that returning owners never verify twice, because existing KYC can be reused through token sharing. So, everything the user shouldn’t have to think about. That’s the definition of invisible.

In practice, it means the provider owns licensing, or a licensed local partner, in every market where money actually moves,  local payment methods, not just cards, because users pay the way their country pays.

It has been revealed that vietnam is the example I keep reaching for. We introduced VietQR there in Q3, and it is already our top payment method in that region at roughly 42% of all transactions — driving a conversion rate close to eight times higher than cards. Same consumers, same product, same pricing. The only variable was letting people pay the way they already pay.

It has been revealed that then provider also need identity and KYC, including the ability to accept verification the partner has already done. Settlement, in and out, with money arriving where it is supposed to on the day it is supposed to.

And it has to run in both directions, not just the buy flow. On-ramp, where a user pays with a local method and receives crypto. Off-ramp, where they sell and cashout to their own bank account.

A lot of products ship the first and treat off-ramp as a secondary problem, and that is precisely the moment a user discovers the money only moves one way.

Sources indicate that for a European fintech, Banxa collects the local payment, exchanges and settles the fiat leg where the partner needs it. We carry the MiCA licence that passports across the EU — so they don’t have to build a crypto licensing and payments stack country by country.

One partner, one compliance review, one integration, both directions. That speed to market is usually why partners choose us.

It has been revealed that – Banxa’s infrastructure supports stablecoin payments across B2B settlement, consumer payments, and cross-border transactions. What is the most overlooked challenge in making stablecoin payments work at scale?

Nobody has ever been excited about reconciliation, and it is the thing that decides whether you have a business.

Industry observers note that A stablecoin transfer settles in seconds. That part is genuinely solved.

Recent findings suggest that what is not solved is everything around it. The fiat leg still moves on banking hours and local scheme rules. You have a bank partner on one side, a chain on the other, and a treasury position sitting between them that has to be funded, hedged and accounted for.

Every transaction has to be matched across those systems, in the right currency, on the right day, with the right fee breakdown, in a form an auditor and a regulator will accept.

The second unglamorous thing is failure handling.

At scale, the interesting work is not the happy path. It is the payment that half-completes.

The most common example is card decline and for many reasons – bank limit, 3D Secure step that timed out etc. In most checkouts that ends the order and the buyer needs to start again, or more often leaves.

In a recent development, then there are bank transfers that arrive three days late with a truncated reference. The refund that has to go back to a card when the crypto has already left.

Users judge you almost entirely on how those cases are handled, and those cases are where most providers quietly fall over.

We recently shipped Payment Method Switch, which lets the buyer change how they pay without losing the order. It separates the order from the payment, so a buyer can move from card to Google Pay without losing the order or redoing verification, and so they see the new method before confirming.

The third challenge is payment method coverage, which sounds like a commercial checklist and is actually an engineering and licensing dependency.

Supporting the way people pay in the US, Nigeria, Australia and Germany means four different integrations, four different fraud profiles and four different regulatory conversations. A switch only works if the alternative payment method is already connected and live for that buyer.

Industry observers note that it matters because this is the layer the user is trusting without knowing it. When the plumbing is right, the experience feels effortless. When it is wrong, it does not feel like a backend concern. It feels like the product lied to them.

– Can KYC be more than compliance — can it actually become a growth advantage in crypto payments?

According to recent reports, yes, and I would go further. KYC is one of the highest-leverage product surfaces in payments. Most teams just never treat it as one.

Look at where users actually drop. It is rarely pricing. It is the verification step.

According to recent reports, someone has decided they want to transact, they have intent, and then they are asked to photograph a document on a screen that does not match the app they were just in. A meaningful share of them never come back.

Sources indicate that that is not a compliance cost. That is a conversion problem.

So the advantage comes from three things.

First, verify once. If a partner has already verified a user to a standard we can rely on, that user should not be asked again. Banxa Native supports exactly this through token sharing, so returning users go straight to payment.

Sources indicate that second, verify proportionately. Not every transaction carries the same risk, so it shouldn’t carry the same friction.

Third, verify natively. No redirect, no third-party screen, no moment where the user wonders who they just handed their passport details to.

Industry observers note that there is a trust argument too. In most of the world, people are more willing to move money with a platform that looks regulated, not less. Verification done well signals that this is a real financial product. Done badly, suggests the opposite.

In a recent development, my advice is to instrument it. Measure drop-off by step. Iterate. Most teams hand it to engineering once and never look again.

– Crypto payments come with a lot of risk, from payment disputes to fraud. Do you the industry underestimates the value of having someone else take on that risk?

In a recent development, badly, yes. And the reason is that the cost of carrying it yourself does not show up as a line item until it is already a problem.

The fiat leg is reversible. The crypto leg is not. A card payment can be disputed months after the asset has left. That gap is where fraud lives.

Sources indicate that so when a platform decides to run its own ramp, they’re usually pricing the integration work. What they are not pricing is the loss rate, the rules engine that has to keep up with it, the team watching it at three in the morning, the bank relationships that get withdrawn when your chargeback ratio crosses a threshold, and the capital you have to hold against all of it.

Those costs are lumpy and they arrive late.

According to recent reports, the real value of transferring that risk is not just the losses avoided. It is focus.

With Banxa Native, the partner owns the experience end to end. We carry the regulated rails and the settlement behind it. They get to spend their engineering time on the things their users actually chose them for.

Sources indicate that risk you have not priced is still risk. Someone is carrying it.

– What’s one thing Web3 companies still see as “just compliance” that should really be treated as a product or growth matter?

Recent findings suggest that market access. Which licences you hold, and therefore which countries you can actually serve, is usually filed under legal. It is the single biggest determinant of your addressable market.

Teams spend enormous effort on acquisition and then discover the funnel is geographically capped. Users arrive, get to the payment step, and find out their country is not supported or their local payment method is not available.

From the user’s point of view, the product simply does not work. From the growth team’s point of view, the conversion rate is mysteriously bad in half the world. Nobody connects that back to a licensing decision made two years earlier.

The same is true of regulatory readiness ahead of a regime change. MiCA is the clearest recent example.

Sources indicate that the companies that treated it as a legal deadline scrambled. The ones that treated it as a product decision kept serving European people without interruption while others paused service. Continuity of access is a growth outcome.

This is also why we think about our licence footprint as product surface area rather than paperwork. Banxa services users across North America, Europe, the UK, Latin America and Asia-Pacific, and is MiCA-authorised as a CASP in the Netherlands. For a partner building on Banxa, that footprint is not a compliance appendix in the contract. It is the list of countries where their product works.

My general rule: if a compliance decision changes who can use your product or how easily, it was never only a compliance decision.

– What development in crypto payments could have the biggest impact on the industry over the next few years?

Stablecoins becoming the default settlement layer for ordinary businesses that have no interest in crypto.

In a recent development, that is the shift. It isn’t necessarily about more people buying digital assets. It’s about companies moving money across borders faster and cheaper, with the stablecoin being an implementation detail they never discuss.

It has been revealed that the future isn’t crypto payments. It’s better payments.

Industry observers note that stablecoin supply has actually contracted since May, from around $310 billion to roughly $286 billion. But payment volume went the other way. Allium reported it at $482 billion in the first nine months of this year, up 45% year on year.

Banks, card networks and large fintechs are integrating this into their products right now.

What makes it transformative is the disappearance, not the technology.

Sources indicate that consumers will keep using the apps and currencies they already trust. The rails underneath will change. Identity handled once, not repeatedly. Settlement in minutes instead of days. Fees people can actually see.

In many emerging markets, this will go further and faster than people in Washington or London expect, because the alternative is genuinely slow.

Digital dollars become the practical choice for savings and cross-border flows, not a theoretical one.

Most customers will never know a stablecoin was involved. That’s the point.

US spot Ether exchange-traded funds are edging toward an uncomfortable milestone. The category has now recorded seven consecutive weeks of net withdrawals, placing it one additional negative week away from matching the longest losing streak identified in the current dataset. That is an especially awkward backdrop for Ethereum supporters who see exchange-traded products as a bridge between the network and traditional investment accounts.

The withdrawal trend does not tell us that institutions have abandoned Ethereum, nor does it measure how much activity is occurring on the blockchain. It does indicate that ETF demand has been persistently soft during a period of broader market stress.

The Block's review of SoSoValue figures put net withdrawals from US spot Ether ETFs at about $398.9 million for the week ending November 13. That marked a seventh consecutive weekly outflow, with cumulative withdrawals of roughly $2.42 billion since late September. Another negative week would tie the eight-week losing streaks the category has previously experienced.

Industry observers note that A single week's figure can be influenced by a handful of large transactions, but seven weeks is long enough to warrant closer examination. NewsBTC's report on the November 9 Ether ETF outflow captured one daily episode; the accumulated weekly data reveals how the pressure has persisted beyond that session.

Owning an Ether ETF share and using Ethereum are fundamentally different activities. A fund investor primarily seeks financial exposure to ETH's price, subject to the product's particular structure and fees. A blockchain user might be paying transaction charges, supplying liquidity, issuing a token or building an application. The two can influence one another over time, but neither provides a complete picture of the other.

For this reason, it would be a mistake to use fund outflows as evidence that smart contracts are no longer being used. A better test of network health also considers transactions, fees, applications, security and adoption. Those indicators require interpretation too, particularly as activity shifts across Ethereum's scaling ecosystem.

The Ether figures arrived in a week when spot Bitcoin ETFs also lost more than $1 billion, and other crypto fund categories largely experienced withdrawals. That broad pattern suggests investors may be reducing digital-asset exposure generally rather than rotating decisively from ETH into BTC. It is a different story from one in which capital leaves one token product but pours into another.

Industry observers note that there is still an important distinction between price losses and fund flows. ETH's falling market value can reduce ETF assets without any redemption, while net withdrawals reflect investor activity through the fund structure. Keeping those measures separate prevents the discussion from exaggerating the selling actually revealed by the data.

The network's DeFi ecosystem continues to evolve, including proposals over how protocols capture fees and share economic value. Aave's recent reserve-factor discussion is one example of the operational debates taking place independently of fund investor sentiment.

It has been revealed that for the next trading week, investors will watch whether Ether funds can interrupt the run of negative flows and whether the change is broad or concentrated in one vehicle. A positive week would not erase the preceding losses, but it would be a measurable sign that some buyers are reconsidering. Until then, the ETF channel remains an obvious pressure point for Ethereum's market narrative.

Crypto investors spend plenty of time staring at Bitcoin charts, but one of the more revealing signals this month may be the amount of dollar-backed stablecoins circulating across the market. Recent data suggests that the combined supply of major stablecoins has contracted materially from its earlier peak. That matters because these tokens are often the cash-like instruments traders use to move money between exchanges, DeFi protocols and new positions.

According to recent reports, A shrinking supply does not automatically cause a market crash, and it certainly does not mean every stablecoin holder has left crypto. It does, however, raise a practical question: is the industry's readily deployable dollar liquidity getting smaller just as prices are falling?

According to recent reports, coinDesk's November 15 market report described the combined stablecoin market retreating toward roughly $244 billion, compared with a peak near $270 billion in May 2026. It also cited Glassnode data indicating a decline of approximately $17 billion over a one-month period. These are market snapshots from particular datasets, not a count of dollars sitting in every crypto trading account.

According to recent reports, the distinction is significant. Stablecoin supply changes when issuers create or redeem tokens, but balances also shift among blockchains, venues and use cases. An on-chain transfer from one exchange to another does not shrink total issuance. A redemption in which tokens are destroyed can do so. Comparing data providers therefore requires consistent definitions and time windows.

Stablecoins serve several functions at once. They can be a temporary refuge during volatile markets, a settlement instrument for trading and a payments rail for companies that want digital dollars without holding Bitcoin or Ether. When aggregate supply grows, traders often interpret that as potential purchasing power entering the ecosystem. When it contracts, one plausible reading is that capital is being withdrawn or used elsewhere.

But supply and demand are not a one-step equation. A dollar token sitting idle in a wallet may be less key to near-term prices than a smaller amount actively circulating through exchanges. Conversely, a market can recover even while headline supply remains flat if existing balances change hands more frequently. The connection is useful, not deterministic.

The business case for stablecoins does not disappear when trading demand weakens. NewsBTC's coverage of Bitso Business's reported payment volumes illustrates how companies use digital dollars for transfers and settlement rather than speculation. Likewise, USDC's rollout through Samsung Wallet on Solana indicates the payments and consumer-access dimension.

That creates an interesting tension. Trading-led demand can ebb even as infrastructure for real-world payments develops. Analysts should therefore ask where supply is shrinking, what people are doing with the remaining balances and whether dollar liquidity on exchanges is tightening faster than demand in payments networks.

Net issuance and redemptions from major issuers are an obvious starting point. Exchange stablecoin balances, cross-chain transfers and DeFi borrowing rates can help provide context, provided their methodology is clear. More importantly, these series should be compared with spot buying and ETF flows rather than used in isolation.

A return to stablecoin growth would not guarantee a rally, but it could indicate that more cash-like capacity is entering the system. Until then, the contraction is another reminder that crypto prices are shaped by the availability of capital as much as by the promise of the underlying technology.

That combination can turn a difficult trading week into a dramatic percentage move, particularly when traders close leveraged positions into weak liquidity.

The central takeaway is that XRP's fall is severe without necessarily being mysterious. A market that is reducing leverage and cash-like liquidity can punish liquid altcoins rapidly. Until there is convincing evidence that that process has run its course, calling an exact bottom would be a guess rather than analysis.

XRP Price Crashes Below $0.90 as Shrinking Stablecoin Supply Drain Crypto Market

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read | Sumber: https://bitcoinist.com/xrp-price-crashes-below-0-90-as-shrinking-stablecoin-supply-drain-crypto-market/

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, XRP price crashes to its lowest price since November 2024, dropping to approximately $0.89 as investors continue pulling capital out of the cryptocurrency market.
  • Recent findings suggest that the payments-focused cryptocurrency has lost approximately 36% of its value this quarter and has struggled to recover since reaching a peak above $3.60 in July 2025.
  • Weaker investment flows and shrinking stablecoin liquidity suggest investors are becoming increasingly cautious, leaving less capital to support demand across the crypto market.

In a recent development, XRP price crashes to its lowest price since November 2024, dropping to approximately $0.89 as investors continue pulling capital out of the cryptocurrency market. The latest decline comes amid growing withdrawals from XRP exchange-traded funds (ETFs) and a significant contraction in the supply of major dollar-backed stablecoins.

Recent findings suggest that the payments-focused cryptocurrency has lost approximately 36% of its value this quarter and has struggled to recover since reaching a peak above $3.60 in July 2025. Its latest decline coincides with broader weakness across digital assets, as Bitcoin and Ethereum have also retreated to price levels last seen in August.

Weaker investment flows and shrinking stablecoin liquidity suggest investors are becoming increasingly cautious, leaving less capital to support demand across the crypto market.

XRP briefly declined to $0.89, marking its weakest level since November 2024. The drop extends a prolonged downward trend that began after the token climbed above $3.60 in July 2025.

It has been revealed that the cryptocurrency has now lost about 36% this quarter, reflecting the broader deterioration in digital asset sentiment. Bitcoin and Ethereum have also experienced substantial declines, with both cryptocurrencies falling to levels last recorded in August. This indicates that XRP’s weakness is unfolding alongside a wider market correction rather than as an isolated event.

Sources indicate that however, XRP’s recent performance highlights the challenges facing altcoins when investors reduce their exposure to riskier digital assets. As market confidence weakens, capital tends to become more selective, putting additional pressure on cryptocurrencies that depend on renewed buying demand to sustain their valuations.

Withdrawals from investment products tracking XRP have added to the selling pressure.

In a recent development, US-listed spot XRP ETFs recorded approximately $19.13 million in net outflows during the week ending November 13, according to SoSoValue data. This represented the largest weekly withdrawal from the products since March 2026.

Despite the recent redemptions, the ETFs have attracted approximately $1.5 billion in cumulative net inflows since launching in November 2025.

That figure highlights the demand the products initially generated, although their relatively modest inflows compared with Bitcoin and Ethereum ETFs suggest that institutional exposure to XRP remains considerably smaller.

According to recent reports, ETF flows remain an important indicator of investor demand. Sustained withdrawals can signal weakening confidence and potentially reduce the buying support available to the underlying cryptocurrency.

Recent findings suggest that pressure on the market extends beyond ETF withdrawals. The combined market capitalization of Tether’s USDT and Circle’s USDC, the two largest dollar-pegged stablecoins, has fallen to approximately $244 billion.

The contraction has accelerated over the past seven weeks, with the combined market capitalization declining from around $260 billion.

According to recent reports, blockchain analytics firm Glassnode highlighted the scale of the reduction, reporting that stablecoin supply had decreased by approximately $17 billion over the previous month. Analysts described this as the steepest monthly decline since 2022.

Stablecoins play an important role in cryptocurrency markets because traders use them to hold dollar-linked value, transfer funds between platforms, and purchase other digital assets.

It has been revealed that consequently, a declining stablecoin supply can indicate that capital is leaving the crypto ecosystem rather than remaining available for future investments. When investors convert stablecoins into traditional currencies, the amount of liquidity potentially available to support cryptocurrency purchases can also decrease.

XRP’s decline below $0.90 highlights the combined impact of weakening investor demand, ETF withdrawals, and reduced liquidity across the cryptocurrency market.

Although the token has experienced substantial losses, its future direction will depend partly on whether capital begins returning to digital assets. A reversal in XRP ETF flows and renewed growth in stablecoin supply could provide indications that investor confidence is improving.

For now, the available data points to a difficult environment for cryptocurrency markets. XRP has fallen to a level last seen in November 2024, while the contraction in stablecoin capitalization suggests that the amount of capital circulating through the sector is also declining.

A sustained recovery may therefore require more than a temporary improvement in XRP’s price. Broader liquidity conditions and renewed institutional demand will likely remain crucial factors in determining whether the cryptocurrency can regain its footing.

Is the sharp contraction in stablecoin supply a temporary liquidity adjustment, or does it signal a deeper withdrawal of capital from the cryptocurrency market?
